In a recent development, rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that A judge remarked he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

According to recent reports, boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg noted.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump noted last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg stated he may glitch rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has mentioned he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

Riviera Travel River Cruise has unveiled a C-suite shift as it prepares for another year of anticipated growth.

Travel industry veteran Vicky Billing has been named president of North America, and Stuart Milan has been elevated to chief commercial officer.

Sources indicate that the company said in a press release that, bringing 30 years of travel industry experience to her fresh role, Billing will oversee Riviera Travel River Cruises’ continued expansion across the U.S. and Canada.

She joins the company’s multinational executive team, reporting directly to CEO Matt Luscombe, and will oversee all aspects of the company’s North American operations.

Billing succeeds Stuart Milan, who has led Riviera Travel River Cruises’ North American operations for the past three years and will return to the UK, promoted to chief commercial officer.

In his new role, Milan will lead Riviera Travel River Cruises’ commercial strategy, driving profitable customer growth across revenue management, commercial planning, trade, loyalty, CRM and digital commerce.

“North America is a key part of Riviera Travel River Cruises’ future, and we have significant ambitions for the market,” mentioned Luscombe.

“Billing is an exceptional commercial leader with a real passion for the travel trade, and I have every confidence she’ll build on the momentum already established and help take our North American business to newly introduced heights.”.

Billing presently serves as Riviera Travel River Cruises’ director of trade, partnerships and loyalty, where she oversees key elements of the organization’s commercial strategy across the UK and Ireland.

“I’m thrilled to take on this opportunity and work alongside our team and partners as we build the next chapter of Riviera’s business in North America,” stated Billing.

“I’m incredibly proud of what the North American team has built over the last three years,” said Milan. “We’ve established a strong foundation for continued growth, supported by a brilliant team and increasingly strong relationships across the travel advisor community.”.

The press release added that the appointments of Billing and Milan are part of a broader evolution of Riviera Travel River Cruises’ executive leadership team.

Will Sarson, at the moment product director, has been promoted to chief brand and product officer, overseeing the organization’s brand, product portfolio and guest proposition.

Robin Shaw, at the moment chief commercial officer, will transition to chief transformation officer, overseeing key strategic initiatives with an immediate focus on the future development of Riviera’s river cruise fleet.

It has been revealed that all changes are effective beginning April 1, 2027. Existing advisor relationships, sales contacts, and trade programs will remain in place throughout the leadership transition.

The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, if you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help.
  • A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, if you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Recent findings suggest that like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

Sources indicate that there are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

Sources indicate that I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can rapidly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

According to recent reports, my recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

It has been revealed that with 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts.

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—notable so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

It has been revealed that the AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

Recent findings suggest that the interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review.

In a recent development, this is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

According to recent reports, it has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

According to recent reports, like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

Industry observers note that with an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

According to recent reports, its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

Recent findings suggest that the Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

Full Noco GB40 Boost Plus Review.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.).

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so owners need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

Recent findings suggest that for motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

Recent findings suggest that this device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

It has been revealed that with 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

Industry observers note that for years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

It has been revealed that with 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

It has been revealed that the Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

Industry observers note that portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

In a recent development, the two most crucial specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

According to recent reports, most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

In a recent development, if you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

In a recent development, yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

According to recent reports, peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two vital. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will matter a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Viking has taken delivery of the Viking Libra, its newest ocean ship, at Fincantieri’s shipyard in Ancona, Italy.

The 998-guest ship will sail itineraries in the Mediterranean and Northern Europe in her inaugural season.

She is a sister to the rest of Viking’s ocean fleet, but unlike the others she has a hybrid propulsion system designed to run on liquefied hydrogen and fuel cells.

The organization’s next ocean ship, the Viking Astrea, is under construction and will have the same system. Viking expects both ships to be operating on hydrogen in 2027.

“The delivery of the Viking Libra is a proud moment for Viking and an vital milestone in our growing ocean fleet,” said Leah Talactac, president and CEO of Viking.

“Together with the Viking Astrea, she will set a new standard for innovation as we bring this technology into operation in 2027 and will allow us to welcome even more curious travelers to explore the world in Viking comfort,” she added.

Under its committed orderbook, Viking expects to take delivery of 25 more river ships by 2030, 10 more ocean ships by 2032 and two more expedition ships by 2031.

Those deliveries would bring the organization’s fleet to 123 river ships in 2030 and 28 ocean and expedition ships in 2032.

It has been revealed that when astronomers first spotted the supernova now designated SN 2026ahvu, it was just one of the dozens detected every day. But scientists soon realized this one was something very special, and they’ve been hustling to study it ever since.

Recent findings suggest that soon after scientists spotted the explosion on November 2, they determined it hadn’t yet peaked in brightness, giving scientists an early glimpse at the event. Even more thrilling, within a day of the explosion’s discovery, astronomers had classified it as a type Ia supernova. These particular outbursts are rare, but they’re astronomical superstars: Scientists use their trademark explosion pattern as a “standard candle” to measure distance into the universe — most notably to discover that the universe’s expansion is accelerating. And to round out a trifecta of reasons to be excited, these blasts rarely occur so close to Earth.

In a recent development, astronomers know type 1a supernovas occur upon the reignition and resulting self-destruction of a white dwarf star, the small cool remnants of a star like the sun that’s too small to become a superdense neutron star or black hole at its demise. Scientists also know that powering back on requires reaching about 1.44 times the mass of the sun, which can occur only if something is giving the white dwarf extra mass.

But scientists aren’t sure what that something is — whether these supernovas are triggered by a second white dwarf or some sort of star that’s still burning. Usually, these explosions occur so far away that astronomers can’t get a good look at where they come from. But SN 2026ahvu is perhaps 50 million light-years or less away from Earth.

“They happen so rarely at this distance that it could hopefully help us figure out why this white dwarf exploded in the first place,” says astronomer Yvette Cendes of the University of Oregon in Eugene, who has been arranging for radio telescopes to observe the outburst.

Sarbadhicary and colleagues have already submitted preliminary findings November 6 at arXiv.org suggesting that the former white dwarf was less than 100 million years old. That’s remarkably young compared with other supernovas of this type, and may help scientists finetune their understanding of these outbursts.

“These explosions have been enduring mysteries for us for decades, and whenever something happens this close, it’s just really exciting,” Sarbadhicary claims.

Tech Report: The 7 Best Pocket Knives for Everyday Tasks and Outdoor Adventures

📅 07 Aug 2017 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4032 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.
  • Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.

Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.

Sources indicate that this guide focuses on functional folding knives with (mostly) approachable price tags that you’ll want to use every day, not place under glass. I test dozens of knives each year, and I’ve chosen my favorites below only from the knives I’ve personally used.

Industry observers note that the Iridium is one of Kershaw’s most popular releases and for good reason. It’s priced modestly with a secure bar lock-out, easy one-handed opening and closing, and it just looks cool. It’s also the sweet spot for most people in terms of size, weight, and style. Not ultralight (just over three ounces), the 6061-T6’s aluminum handle and slim profile keep it barely noticeable in your pocket.

When testing, I found the 4.5-inch length was great for my medium-sized hands and shouldn’t be too big or small for any hands—or jobs. Kershaw offers low- and mid-priced production knives made in China, but they follow up with high-quality control in their Oregon facilities and consistently deliver designs that just work.

At the core of the Iridium series is a secure, Benchmade-style crossbar lock, and while there are models that veer into Benchmade prices, many models, including the original, can be had for less than $100.

The Iridium is easy to use—opening with a smooth action, activated by the thumb stud opener. Though it’s not spring-assisted, the blade flicks open fast without resistance. Closing is similarly smooth—just pull down on the crossbar lock and close with a finger, or hold upright and let the blade fall shut. I usually prefer the satisfying speed of a flipper, but the smooth action of the Iridium’s thumb stud opening rivals the Benchmade Bugout’s, and it quickly grew on me.

It has been revealed that the D2 steel used in the original, which offers decent edge retention and durability, is common in lower-cost knives but can rust if you abuse it. A compromise option: Go with the black oxide-coated D2 blade which keeps all but the cutting edge sealed off from rust. The look on all these versions of the Iridium matches the modern design features, and the only drawback of how smooth and slick the knife looks is that it’s not the best for operating in wet or muddy conditions where grip could become an issue.

Full Kershaw Iridium Pocket Knife Review.

In a recent development, coast is one of several Oregon-based knife manufacturers (the company also sells a wide range of flashlights and headlamps) to offer a range of budget-friendly folding pocket knives. My favorite from their lineup is the fairly small but robust Contra, which has an all-metal build and a lifetime warranty despite the low cost. The wharncliffe blade, made from a softer 7CR17 steel, dulls faster than high-end steels but has the benefit of being easy to sharpen at home.

The wharncliffe blade gives you the utility of a box cutter blade but much more versatility as you retain a decent point for puncturing tasks, and I’ve come to prefer it for everyday carry over more traditional drop point shapes. Coast adds durability to its budget steel with a black oxide coating that I found doesn’t scratch easily. The knife is a full stainless-steel build with a good-looking stonewash finish on the handle which integrates the frame lock system.

In a recent development, the flipper opening is fast and satisfying for knife fidgeters but it’s usually safer to employ a two-handed closure. Given the overseas production and ultra-low sticker price, this pocket knife’s durability could be a potential concern, but I’ve used mine roughly near-daily for more than a year and haven’t broken or chipped the blade. It still looks fresh.

Sources indicate that benchmade is an American knife brand based in Oregon with a loyal following for its premium production pocket knives. Known for lightweight designs, modern materials, and innovation, the brand has produced many favorites—but my top pick is the Benchmade 535 Bugout.

To me, the Bugout captures what Benchmade does best: an ultralight folder that’s still strong, well-built, and made with high-quality steel (and the same holds true with the Benchmade 533 Mini Bugout). Some might argue the Benchmade Osborne 940 is the brand’s most iconic knife, but I reach for the Bugout every time—especially for hunting, camping, backpacking, or backcountry skiing, where weight matters.

Industry observers note that the design is modern without feeling overly tactical. It’s streamlined with a simple profile and a practical drop-point blade. The textured Grivory scales—glass-reinforced plastic—keep weight incredibly low while maintaining rigidity.

At under two ounces and just 0.42 inches thick, the Bugout is barely noticeable in a pocket, making it ideal for long outdoor trips. For those who don’t like the Grivory feel, there are versions with aluminum or carbon-fiber scales and a range of steel options.

Operation is another highlight. Benchmade’s Axis Lock uses a spring-loaded crossbar that allows easy one-handed opening and closing from either hand while keeping fingers out of the blade path. The mechanism is simple, strong, and easy to maintain—I even built one myself at the Benchmade factory and found it intuitive without instructions.

In terms of cutting performance, my Bugouts arrived razor-sharp out of the box. I prefer the standard S30V steel because it balances edge retention with easier sharpening in the field, though higher-end options like S90V are available if you want longer-lasting sharpness. S30V is also tough and corrosion-resistant, which suits hard outdoor use.

It has been revealed that benchmade’s lifetime warranty and sharpening service add real long-term value. The Bugout isn’t cheap, but with its reliability, ultralight design, and customization options, it’s easy to recommend—especially for outdoor enthusiasts or anyone wanting a high-quality everyday carry knife.

Full Benchmade Bugout 535 Review.

Case is one of the original American knife brands still standing and, unlike many of their competitors that have shipped production to China, most of Case’s knives are still designed and produced in Bradford, Pennsylvania.

Whether or not that matters to you, Case makes great knives, and while they sell a lot of nostalgic designs unchanged for a century, the Kinzua is one of their modern EDC offerings that departs from the Case aesthetic with an all-metal build, flipper action, sharp lines, and a tanto blade.

Industry observers note that the satin-finished S35VN steel blade is a good compromise of hardness and edge durability while still being fairly easy to sharpen at home. It also has a lightly weathered look that should hide abuse well. One note is that, while extremely sturdy, the all-metal frame-lock design is pretty stiff to close out of the box.

Releasing the frame lock requires some force and closing requires a few moves. With a little practice I was able to comfortably operate it one-handed, but folks with smaller or weaker hands may not feel the same.

Industry observers note that the Bugout is one of our favorite Benchmade folders, and we recommend it above as our Best Lightweight pocket knife. But the brand’s newly introduced Bugout Vapyr variant is different enough to warrant its own place on the podium. The most noticeable difference is the width. The original Bugout is featherlight at two ounces, but the Vapyr gets that down to 1.72 ounces and shrinks the width by 3 mm, which is very obvious in the hand.

It’s impressive engineering, but practically, it takes a knife that was barely noticeable in the pocket and makes it borderline undetectable. It costs $375—nearly double the regular Bugout—so this is for folks with fewer budget constraints who are willing to spend for the lightest, thinnest folder that doesn’t compromise on utility and durability.

Sources indicate that part of that price jump can be chalked up to Benchmade swapping in MagnaCut steel for the S30V in the baseline Bugout. S30V is already a great blade steel with high corrosion resistance and incredible edge retention, and Benchmade has come to be known for using it. But MagnaCut is a step above on both metrics.

In a recent development, the other substantial change is the Axis lock, which remains functionally the same but swaps in a latest stepped slide in place of the longstanding metal button. It’s a minor swap that first-time Benchmade buyers likely won’t even notice. But having used Axis locks for years, I much prefer the new slide.

There’s a subtle internal change from an omega spring to a tension spring. It didn’t feel different when I used it side by side with the original Bugout, but Benchmade notes the tension springs have a longer lifespan. It’s worth noting that while better durability is welcome considering the price tag, all Benchmade knives have a lifetime warranty (and lifetime sharpening service) if a spring were to fail.

According to recent reports, one drawback from the original Bugout is that, at least with the Bugout Vapyr I tested, the pivot is much tighter and requires more force to open. You can open a Bugout one of two ways. One, you can use the thumb stud to spin the blade out into the locked-open position. Alternatively, you can pull the Axis lock open and flick the blade open. This second option requires a touch of timing and gets harder with the Vapyr’s tighter pivot, though I didn’t find the thumb stud actuation any more challenging in the Vapyr.

Full Benchmade Bugout Vapyr Review.

In a recent development, I’ve been looking for a good automatic pocket knife for years, and the CRKT Twist Tighe Automatic is the only one that I’ve found that doesn't feel like a novelty knife. It’s compact, lightweight, fun to use, and practical enough for everyday carry while still delivering the fun factor that draws many people to automatic knives in the first place.

Automatics, often called switchblades, are popular with knife enthusiasts because they’re inherently fidget-friendly. The Twist Tighe is an out-the-front (OTF) automatic, meaning the blade deploys straight out of the front of the handle. Besides being undeniably cool, I find the operation safer than many folding knives because it’s harder to accidentally place your fingers in the blade’s path when opening and closing.

The highlight is its smooth double-action mechanism. Sliding the spine button forward fires the blade; pulling it back retracts it. Many automatics I’ve tried are either stiff or inconsistent, but the Twist Tighe feels smooth and reliable even after repeated use. That ease of operation also makes it surprisingly approachable for people who aren’t experienced with knives.

The design comes from Canadian knife designer Brian Tighe, and the handle’s raised spiral grooves are a distinctive touch fans of his work will recognize. In the all-black configuration, the knife looks sleek and slightly dramatic without becoming impractical. My version features a tanto blade with a black titanium nitride finish, while other configurations of the Twist Tighe have double-edged blades and more colorful scale options.

Size and weight are also substantial differences from other automatics. At just 1.6 ounces with a 2.65-inch blade and about a 4-inch closed length, it’s remarkably small for an OTF knife and easy to carry daily. However, people with large hands may find it a bit compact.

Sources indicate that overall, the Twist Tighe combines premium materials like CPM MagnaCut steel with one of the smoothest actions I’ve experienced. If you’re looking for a compact, high-quality OTF automatic for everyday carry, it’s an excellent choice.

The CRKT Minimalist Nessmuk combines the classic look of an outdoor blade with everyday convenience—plus there are several carry options for its sheath. It’s also surprisingly affordable for the build quality, priced at well under $100, with 12C27 stainless steel that keeps the cost down while providing corrosion resistance and easy sharpening.

Another thing in its favor is its versatility beyond hunting season. Thanks to its broad belly, it excels at slicing food, carving wood, breaking down cardboard, and cutting cordage.

With three deep finger choils in the G10 handle, it remained comfortable in hand while I tested it, and the textured scales provided better grip than many larger knives with smoother handles. That may not be the case for folks with larger hands, however, considering the size of the handle. Still, for most people, it’s an excellent choice for a fixed blade that can handle general tasks.

Testing and reviewing knives is a mostly subjective affair, despite all the ink spilled over steel hardness and the trade-offs between edge retention and durability. And with that in mind, I should highlight that these selections are made by one person and thus subject to my personal biases when it comes to pocket knives.

While I’ve developed many idiosyncratic preferences over more than a decade of knife reviewing and 40 years plus of knife-using, the substantial one is that I am a knife user before a knife enthusiast. I can appreciate a “cool” knife design as much as any other knife nut that owns hundreds of knives, but I’m partial to folding designs that work well, fit my hand, and make my life easier in their role as an essential daily use tool.

We patch this guide multiple times throughout the year, and I’m constantly testing new pocket knives to look for new models that are worthy enough to unseat the favorites—and I don’t do that lightly. Year-round testing allows for longer-term use instead of a couple days of fidgeting with a blade and writing up a review. Most of the pocket knives featured here have been in my pocket on and off for months if not years, tackling everyday tasks as well as seasonal jobs such as butchering an elk or deer (if I’m lucky). We’ve included knives from the downright cheap to prohibitively expensive, but all the knives featured are ones we feel deliver good value considering the price tier.

As a baseline for any new knife, I check the factory edge for sharpness, look for corrosion resistance with a saltwater bath and air drying, and (when feasible) disassemble the knife to better understand the lock and open/close mechanisms. After beating up a knife for a while, I also sharpen the blade with stones with an angle guide to find out just how easy it is to return the blade to sharp. One of my favorite tests is handing a knife to friends and strangers to see how regular people react to opening and closing one for the first time, since I spend more time with knives than most.

Choosing blade steel is where knife geeks can get into the weeds. There are trade-offs, though, with any type of steel. Broadly speaking, if you go with a softer steel it means the blade may get dull more easily but it's also easier to sharpen. Harder types of steel hold an edge longer but might be trickier for novices to sharpen at home.

Recent findings suggest that steel characteristics also affect how prone a blade will be to rusting; however, most decent modern pocket knives use a steel that’s rust-resistant enough that it won't require lots of special care. Almost all knives’ product pages will list the type of steel used, and if they don’t, it’s likely a budget knife. If you can’t find the steel online, check knife marketplace sites such as BladeHQ for the make and model.

Here are the highlights for some of the more common pocket knife steel types:.

Recent findings suggest that handle material is also an crucial choice. Wood is less common these days and less durable than steel or lighter, more durable synthetic materials like G10 and carbon fiber. Still, you may prefer the feel and look of wood despite the drawbacks. Steel is strong and durable but adds weight which can be a positive or a negative depending on how you use the knife and what you prefer hanging on your pocket.

In a recent development, A knife’s dimensions and weight affect the fit in your hand and ease of use. In general, bigger hands won’t like tiny knives and vice versa, but how and where you carry a knife impact your preferences for size and weight. If you’re an office executive, you may not want an oversized, obvious blade for daily carry, while working on a farm or in the trades, you might prefer a bigger, burlier blade to stand up to prying tasks and day-to-day abuse.

It has been revealed that the action of a pocket knife can play an outsized role in your appreciation for it. I routinely test a lot of folding knives and find the knives I reach for most often are ones that are the most (subjectively) satisfying—and that I can easily operate one-handed when my off hand is busy doing something else. If you carry it long enough, you’ll get proficient with most any knife, but each of these common mechanisms has its strengths and weaknesses to consider.

In the previous century, secure locking mechanisms weren’t common, but today they’re expected if not universal. Classic knives, such as Case’s beloved Stockman and Victorinox’s iconic Swiss Army Knife, use slip joints, which hold the blade open but don’t truly lock. Because of the increased safety of a locking blade, I recommend choosing a pocket knife with some kind of a locking mechanism. If you are comfortable with a slip joint or other non-locking blade and enjoy the style, by all means, buy one. Note that your choice of lock typically dictates how you close the knife, so this will have a major impact on how easy it is to operate.

Industry observers note that if cost is a major factor for you, it will quickly narrow the range of options. Knives can range in cost from just a few dollars to hundreds or even thousands for custom and limited edition options from celebrated knifemakers. Most people, however, will be looking at what are called “production knives”—models that are mass-produced, usually in a factory instead of by hand from individual knifemakers. While these blades can still run up to $500 or so, the range is much tighter as the cost to produce is lower.

In a recent development, knives for less than about $20 will usually feature softer, cheaper steels and inexpensive handles. These knives may have less quality control than pricier models, but you can still get a decent knife from an established manufacturer any day of the week for less than $50. For example, the cheapest knife I recommend costs about $25.

According to recent reports, choosing a pocket knife with harder carbon steel will usually push the price closer to $100 or more. Go past that $100 price point, and you’re paying for specific designs, brand names, and other personal preferences, but you’ll start to see diminishing returns as far as raw functionality.

Recent findings suggest that in the United States, carrying most pocket knives won’t break any laws. But each state has its own rules that might restrict the specific pocket knives you can legally carry. Many states have prohibitions on certain automatic knives, on blade length, and even on whether or not you can carry certain knives concealed.

Sources indicate that the American Knife and Tool Institute has a helpful state-by-state guide to knife laws you can consult. Traveling abroad brings an even wider range of regulations, as some countries such as Austria have almost no restrictions while Norway (despite a rich knifemaking heritage) has an outright ban on carrying knives in urban areas.

In a recent development, possibly. First, not all pocket knives are the same. The legal definition of pocket knives may vary across states and at the federal level which can impact shipment and receipt.

It has been revealed that most states also have some kind of restrictions on what knives you can carry on your person. Even in wild west Colorado where I live, it is illegal to carry a blade longer than 3.5 inches “concealed” which would include “in your pocket.” In New York state where I grew up, switchblades are illegal and you must be a U.S. citizen to even own a knife, but there are no concealed carry restrictions. Check your state laws here.

In a recent development, outside of local laws, consider how a knife fits in your hand. A knife that feels tiny and awkward to someone with large hands might be perfect for someone else. If you’re not already a regular pocket knife carrier, stop into an outdoors store where you can handle a wide range of knives and see what feels good. Most people will feel comfortable with blades in the 2.5- to 3-inch range, though folks with larger hands may want something bigger.

Sources indicate that I’ll start with a caution—that you may not want a surgically sharp pocket knife. Because I use my pocket knife so frequently and casually, I don’t like to be as cautious as you have to be with an ultra-sharp blade.

Industry observers note that I experimented with carrying a replaceable blade knife for a few months and I ended up giving myself several minor but annoying slices. That stated, any knife will eventually require sharpening. Most pocket knives have a fairly obtuse 20-degree or higher blade angle, which makes them less challenging to sharpen yourself.

In a recent development, knife sharpening is a skill that’s not easy to master (learn how here), but there are tools available to help. While whetstone sharpening is soothing in a Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance sort of way, you probably already have a pull-through sharpener somewhere (check kitchen drawers).

In a recent development, these sharpeners aren’t the perfect sharpening solution, but they’re relatively idiot-proof and good enough to perk up your blade. If all of this sounds like something you’ll never bother with, there are lots of mail-in sharpening services such as The Sharp Brothers, who will professionally sharpen your blades for a fee. Also, many manufacturers offer similar services. Benchmade, for example, has a LifeSharp program that gives you free sharpening for any Benchmade knife. Some manufacturers such as Kershaw also offer blade replacement (often for a fee) if you’ve broken or otherwise damaged your blade beyond repair.

It has been revealed that this is both a surprisingly common and difficult-to-answer question. Obviously personal budget comes into play, but so do your preferences. Despite considering myself a pocket knife enthusiast, I carried a cheap pocket knife from Walmart for years that cost me literally $1. The firm raised the price to $2 at some point. Those knives would rust at the hinge, but they did the trick and were great for putting in my checked luggage. I wouldn’t worry about losing it at my destination and wouldn’t cry if the TSA took it.

While I can’t recommend buying $2 knives in good conscience for most circumstances, quality options such as the Coast Contra recommended above can be had for under $20. If you’re new to knives, start out with something cheaper, definitely under $50, until you develop strong opinions about the pocket knife you prefer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Carnival Cruise Line is expanding its onboard beverage packages to two of its private destinations: Celebration Key and RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay.

According to a recent press release, passengers will be able to order drinks included in their packages at the destinations starting in February 2027.

Sources indicate that the extension will be available for Carnival’s CHEERS!, CHEERS! Zero Proof™, Bottomless Bubbles™ and CHEERS! Social drink packages.

Carnival stated the move will “give guests who purchase these packages greater value for their vacation dollars.”.

The change brings Carnival closer to other cruise lines that already extend their beverage packages to private islands.

While some brands, including Norwegian Cruise Line and MSC Cruises, limit the land extension to their premium packages, others include all packages.

In related news, Carnival also announced the first details of the newly introduced Carnival Destiny, which will enter service in 2029, as well as an order for two smaller newbuilds.

The company is also investing in Paradise Collection, its portfolio of private destinations across the Caribbean and the Bahamas.

Celebration Key will see the biggest investment, with a significant expansion project set to take place over the next few years.

The private destination in Grand Bahama will see its daily capacity increased by 6,000 guests, with the expansion divided into two phases.

The first will be ready in 2028 and will feature a heated, beach-entry pool with a swim-up bar, as well as six waterslides, a dry climbing structure and a drenching bucket for children.

In 2030, the second phase will add a major water park with 18 waterslides, a lazy river with float-up bars and swim-in/swim-out cabanas, as well as a fresh exclusive area with an infinity pool, more beach access and new dining and bar concepts.

Carnival noted that, with six exclusive destinations in five countries, its lineup is the largest in the industry.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

Industry observers note that “I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

In a recent development, working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he mentioned.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are at the moment selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers mentioned, describing it as “deplorable.”.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech tech giant Oracle.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Royal Caribbean has announced the appointments of Greg Nicholas as senior director, Singapore, North & South APAC, and Megan Smith as head of marketing, Singapore, North & South APAC.

The appointments strengthen the company’s leadership team as it continues to expand across Asia Pacific, Royal Caribbean stated in a statement.

Based in Singapore, Nicholas will lead commercial operations across North and South APAC markets, while Smith will oversee regional marketing strategy and execution.

Together, they will play a key role in supporting Royal Caribbean’s continued growth, enhancing commercial capabilities and delivering the world’s best family vacations to guests across the region, Royal Caribbean added.

“These appointments come at an important time as we continue to grow our business and expand deployment across Asia. We are further strengthening our regional commercial capabilities and bringing our teams closer together to capture the opportunities ahead,” mentioned Ben Bouldin, president of Greater China and managing director Asia, Royal Caribbean.

According to the statement, Nicholas brings nearly a decade of experience with the company, having held a range of commercial leadership roles across Australia and New Zealand.

Most recently, he served as director, commercial planning for AUNZ, helping shape commercial and deployment strategies across the region.

Smith joins the Singapore team after leading marketing initiatives across China, EMEA, and the UK and Ireland.

The company said her experience spans brand strategy, customer marketing, partnerships, loyalty and trade marketing.

The appointments come as Royal Caribbean expands its presence in Singapore and Asia Pacific, with the Navigator of the Seas offering a year-long season in the market through October 2027, followed by the Quantum of the Seas.
