Tech Report: Nomad Citizen: A Upcoming Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

📅 18 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured.
  • The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that.
  • I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just rolled out what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health initiative, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just rolled out what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single initiative. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really swiftly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

Industry observers note that I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

According to recent reports, for those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the initiative can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

It has been revealed that if you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

According to recent reports, health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Sources indicate that visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Sources indicate that everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

According to recent reports, for health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking upcoming income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This latest Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

Tech Report: Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov.
  • Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec.
  • That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

Recent findings suggest that but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

Several senators leaving the meeting mentioned the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

According to recent reports, that was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., mentioned Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

Recent findings suggest that “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

Industry observers note that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

In a recent development, sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, noted, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she remarked.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday stated at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

In a recent development, “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

Sources indicate that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., remarked Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

Sources indicate that several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve mentioned many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

In a recent development, that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who stated he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

In a recent development, kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

Sources indicate that “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he mentioned. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he remarked. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but mentioned, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

Recent findings suggest that “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he mentioned. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

Industry observers note that sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

Sources indicate that “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan stated.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

It has been revealed that “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., remarked, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

The Golden Rules of Affordable Family Travel, Illustrated by Mona Chalabi

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that my first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014.
  • It has been revealed that take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions.
  • As we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in Upcoming York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that my first Thanksgiving was a lavish 12-person dinner in Connecticut in 2014. I had moved to the US in March of that year and had planned on working from home until a friend generously invited me to go spend the day with her family; an act of unguarded openness that I’ve realized is one of the many things that differentiates Americans from Brits. As soon as we got off the train in Cambridge, Massachusetts, I realized that even though my friend lived in a nasty, overcrowded apartment in Brooklyn, she came from a family that had immense wealth. After dinner, as I helped wash plates in the kitchen, my friend’s mum asked her why she wouldn’t just move into the lovely building they had bought for her. She turned beet red and handed me another dirty plate without looking at me.

It has been revealed that take it from an immigrant: this holiday is full of weird contradictions. Of course, there’s the annual reminder of colonization which requires a careful forgetting of the people who have been colonized. And then there’s the financial aspect of it. At first blush, it seems like the least capitalist holiday of the year—there isn’t the expense of Christmas or Hanukkah gift-giving or the extravagance of Halloween candy. Yet the holiday also marks the start of one of the year's busiest travel seasons when families are taking great expense to reunite, vacation, and explore outside of their every day lives.

As we approach the last Thursday of November, with money very much on our minds, the below well-traveled parents share their hard-won wisdom on pulling off affordable family travel—including how to find treasure in Upcoming York City’s Chinatown without paying an arm and a leg, seek out free entertainment in the streets of Oaxaca, and embrace the joys of accessible public transportation in Europe. All of these stories say something about the wealth of the person writing it, whether or not they wanted to reveal that information. I’m obsessed with getting to the truth about someone’s class (it’s why I wrote my book on the subject), and so these family dispatches, which serve as equal parts advice and confession, are a treat I’ll come back to when I’m not busy washing a rich family’s plates. —Mona Chalabi, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer and illustrator.

Keep reading for the tips and tricks of affordable family travel, road-tested by the experts and illustrated by Mona Chalabi.

Industry observers note that I know the secret to parenting and I’m willing to share it: snacks. Snacks are everything—they’re an activity, a mood changer, and a window into culture for kids. Hit a local farmers market on your first day or if you’re somewhere truly out of their comfort zone even a local convenience store—like 7-Eleven in Tokyo—for something that can feel both familiar and novel. If your hotel room has a refrigerator you can store any pre-cut fruit that you buy, or opt for items that don’t require refrigeration like apples, bananas, and clementines. Bring a lightweight backpack, refill each morning, and watch the hangry meltdowns (mostly) vanish. —Dana Kravis, global executive director, CNT video.

Recent findings suggest that last December in London, we stayed in a quaint Airbnb in Primrose Hill and explored different neighborhoods on foot. When our kids, then eight and three, got tired, we hopped on a double-decker bus and headed upstairs, hoping for front seats. Suddenly, getting home became an amusement park ride: Christmas lights, bustling streets, panoramic views. The kids loved it; as a photographer, I loved the vantage point. London caps daily bus fares when you use the same card or phone, and children under 11 ride free. We’ve done this in Singapore, too. Our rule: skip the sightseeing tour (or Uber) and make public transportation part of the family adventure. —Tanveer Badal, photographer.

Sources indicate that breakfast is where family vacations are made, or broken. My moody teenagers can’t be pried out of bed no matter what city they wake up in, so instead of wringing my uncaffeinated hands and hoping to get us all on the same schedule, I just bring my own breakfast, coffee included. Whether in Paris, Rome, or a tent, you will find me hand-grinding my coffee beans, brewing a pour-over, and snacking on a pastry left over from the previous day while I peruse headlines. Avoiding the time and expense of a sit-down breakfast, and indulging in a bit of morning self-care, means we can focus on the adventures and meals we are actually going to remember. —Chris Morocco, food director of Bon Appétit and Epicurious.

Recent findings suggest that my parents and I meet in Aruba every winter for a family vacation that’s warm and relaxing when everyone else is cold and miserable. It’s a classic only child/parents trip where we spend most of our time eating lunch talking about where we’re going to eat dinner. We spend our days mostly just reading parallel to each other. I’ve never been an e-reader user, so I have to bring several physical books to read to get me through the week. The key is that my mom and I have some shared taste in books, so when we finish our own we can swap and save ourselves buying extra books (or lugging even heavier luggage through the airport). —Alison Leiby, comedian and writer.

According to recent reports, finding creative ways to entertain wiggly one-year-olds with limited attention spans can be daunting, but it turns out all you need is a good window. From London to California, staying in rooms on low floors with windows overlooking lots of activity below has resulted in seemingly endless engagement—waving at commuters striding by or golfers strolling a few feet away? Bonus points if the room has curtains with electronic controls—that guarantees an extra hour of ooohs and aaahs, at least. —Sarah Khan, contributing editor.

Industry observers note that I have a thing for seeing “The World’s Biggest or Oldest,” and so here we were at Missouri’s Oldest Wooden Suspension Bridge. “Don’t tell your mom,” I mentioned to my kids, because any bridge that was built from wood during the Civil War should be treated with caution—and, also, all good dad stories start that way. We started up the van, piled everyone in, and began the adventure. The wood cracked and echoed as we drove over the river. It sounded like a popping spinal cord. We swayed, and for a moment, I actually questioned myself. I should have just taken them to the park. Thankfully, I can now confidently say that Missouri’s oldest wooden suspension bridge can hold the weight of a mini-van. —Shannon Carpenter, humorist.

Sources indicate that new York is an expensive city and the best way to keep it cheap is to throw petty cash at it. Instead of buying tickets to an overpriced kid’s experience, I give my children a few twenty dollar bills and take them to Chinatown for a shopping spree. They love the atrocious arcade, and there are fake Labubus, squishy dumplings, a plastic “jade” green dragon that my son now keeps on his bedside, and a 'gold' necklace my daughter thinks is treasure. —Stephanie Danler, author.

As a seasoned travel writer, I know that any hotel that’s gotten media coverage is often pushing $1,000/night. My trick for affordable family lodging is loading up Google maps, figuring out which area we’re going to stay in, and picking a cheerful place with good reviews in the $250 range. It’s almost never one you’ve heard of, but they’re always clean and cheerful, usually family-owned, and we always leave with major hugs and promises to keep in touch. That doesn’t happen at the Georges V. My kids (12 and 8) loved a converted windmill in Rome, a townhouse two blocks from the Rijksmuseum and—most recently—an orange grove near Siracusa where they spent so much time chasing the owner’s cats they even forgot Wi-Fi existed. A steal at any price! —Priyanka Mattoo, filmmaker and author.

In a recent development, people tell you about a million things you “need” before your baby is born, but there's one that has come in the most handy, and I've had a true love/hate relationship with it since day one: A travel car seat. After a ton of research—some may say over-research—we bought a Maxi Cosi Romi. It's rated high for safety, but it's also easy to strap into a car and also an airplane. We always bring it on the airplane, and that's where the headache comes in. While the Maxi Cosi Romi is considered lightweight, it's also big and bulky, and the only way to get it through the airport and onto the plane is by wearing it in a special backpack. I'm pretty sure that I'm one of the most annoying people in any airport as I'm walking through it since I can't really see if I'm bumping into people in the TSA line or getting to the gate. The thing is that, after I considered the numbers, it's actually a really wise investment because most rental car places charge anywhere from $10 to $15 a day to rent a car seat, so we've already started saving money because of it. Now, that's about a hundred or more dollars we're not spending when we go out of town and bring the Maxi. It's wildly annoying and inconvenient, and I look like I'm wearing a jetpack as I'm walking through the airport, but it's worth it. —Jason Diamond, 'Figuring' family columnist at The Cut.

I️ live in Brooklyn where people leave really good stuff out on the street. Once I️ found one of those giant extra storage containers you put on top of your car. I️ haven't found the time to figure out how to put it on top of the car; it's been taking up valuable space in my home for over a year. The other day, I️ found another one that looked even fancier. I️ dragged it home. One day, ideally before our car gets too old to work anymore, I️ will figure this out, then get rid of the extra one somehow (do I️ need to call 311?). After that, my husband, our two kids, our dog, our parakeets and I️ will pack up everything we could possibly need to rent a house somewhere for a week or two. I️ have my eye on Block Island or Martha's Vineyard. —Liana Finck, cartoonist and author.

According to recent reports, from bustling markets to neighborhood festivals, I've learned that some of the best family entertainment happens in the streets. In Oaxaca, my four-year-old was mesmerized by calendas, raucous community processions with brass bands, towering puppets called monos de calenda, and rag-covered revelers known as tiliches. Paradegoers tossed my kid candy, fireworks exploded overhead, and the party raged late into the night. We didn't pay a peso. Before booking pricey family activities, research local festivals, celebrations, and public performances. Sometimes the most exciting show in town is happening right on the sidewalk. —Ashlea Halpern, contributing editor.

It has been revealed that on our last family vacation to Rajasthan, a passionfruit lassi from our five-star hotel nearly ruined the trip. We’re talking emergency roadside bathroom stops and several days of Zofran. We’ve been taking our kids—Vijay, Vik, and Meera—to Rajasthan since they were babies; they’re teenagers now. And we’ve learned one unexpected lesson: the sickest we’ve ever been in India was after eating at our five-star hotel. More than once.

So we’ve adopted a fresh philosophy: pack the right medicine and embrace street food. In Jaipur, Vineet Sharma, founder of Jaipur Walks, led us on a street food tour around the bustling market, introducing us to piping-hot pyaaz kachori and creamy, saffron-rich kulfi. His advice? Choose clean stalls with high turnover, and favor food cooked fresh and served hot over raw offerings. At busy stalls, food is often prepared continuously and served straight from the heat—sometimes a more reassuring bet than a meal at a luxury hotel or high-end restaurant. And if your stomach’s going to revolt, at least make the meal memorable. —Christine Chitnis, author and photographer.

Industry observers note that this may not be the most popular piece of advice, and I doubt it'll be the most obvious: take your kids overseas during school time. Hear me out: the longer you can stretch your child's travels beyond the limited school holidays when ticket prices always soar, the better for your wallet. Of course, every parent needs to set their own boundary on what and how much school their kind can miss in the name of travel but I feel, especially at a young age, the benefits of the trip outweigh the additional days in the classroom. As I am writing this, I am preparing to leave tomorrow with my first grader for Italy for a week. We are cooking up intends to take our two kids on a long haul trip to the southern hemisphere that'll cut into a week of school. I have heard from more than one expert that Disney especially, should be done when your kids are young, and outside normal school holidays if you want to get great value. I don't do it often but I do balance the guilt with rules—we have to read every day, and do exercises from a homework packet to keep on top of the basics. One day, and soon, I know I won't want to do this much more. But for now, I'm taking every chance to do so. —Erin Florio, global features director.

Tech Report: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov.
  • Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen.
  • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola mentioned in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

In a recent development, she entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

According to recent reports, but the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has stated she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

According to recent reports, trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

Recent findings suggest that the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer mentioned in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

#146901. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

📅 01 Apr 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (940 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Godsavethepoints ↗ Open Full Page

What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

📅 01 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Godsavethepoints

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight.
  • Sources indicate that for businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about.
  • Industry observers note that well, a lot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

Sources indicate that for businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Industry observers note that well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

In a recent development, the first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

Industry observers note that but I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

According to recent reports, I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

According to recent reports, and this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

Industry observers note that the big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

From now through November 30, you can use the ITA Airways Black Friday promo code CYBERDAYS to score 10% off your base fare for one-way or round-trip tickets departing from the US and going to any ITA Airways destination, for travel from December 1, 2026, to March 22, 2027. Recent findings suggest that there are three membership tiers: Frequent Traveller, Senator, and HON Circle. To achieve Frequent Traveller status, guests must earn 650 points and 325 qualifying points in a calendar year. While you’ll earn regular points when flying on all travel classes across an array of Star Alliance airlines, you can only earn qualifying points when you fly on the following airlines: Air Dolomiti, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, Discover Airlines, Eurowings, ITA Airways, Lufthansa, SWISS, Croatia Airlines, LOT Polish Airlines, and Luxair. Benefits include business lounge access, the opportunity to get up to 50% extra miles that can be redeemed for additional rewards, and increased free baggage allowance.

Sources indicate that to achieve Senator status, you must earn 2,000 points and 1,000 qualifying points in return for benefits like first-class check-in, priority boarding, and access to Senator/Star Alliance Gold lounges. As for HON Circle? That costs a whopping 6,000 HON points, which can only be earned by flying business or first class on select airline partners. Perks include access to first-class lounges, exclusive chauffeur and transfer services, and free upgrade vouchers. Miles & More members can also earn up to 25% cashback on intercontinental award travel bookings departing from the US, or up to 15% cashback on general intercontinental itineraries.

According to recent reports, those between the ages of 12 and 25 are eligible for ITA Airways youth fares to help cut down on travel costs. Discounts will be applied directly to your booking when made through this page (it will say “youth fare” under the correct price), and you’ll be able to follow through with your booking as usual.

Offers are only eligible for those who will be 12–25 years old on the date of travel, and passengers may need to prove their eligibility upon boarding (so have your ID ready). This discounted fare is only valid for flights to destinations in Europe and is not applicable to unaccompanied minors under 14; 14-year-olds may travel unaccompanied to domestic locations only.

If your ITA Airways discount code isn’t working, don’t fret. There are a couple of things you can do to get your code up and working. The first thing to check is whether you’re applying your promo code to the correct fare class—ITA Airways discount codes are often class-specific, so for example, basic economy fares may not apply. Also be sure to check your discount code to confirm your proposed booking is for an eligible route, not during a blackout date, and hasn’t expired. If all else fails, don’t forget to double-check your code for any spacing errors or mistaken capitalizations.

It's also worth keeping in mind that, like for most other products and services, discount codes do not work on taxes and fees. #146896. Cristian Mungiu’s Latest Drama Fjord Plunges Into the Depths of Coastal Norway

Cristian Mungiu’s Latest Drama Fjord Plunges Into the Depths of Coastal Norway

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television demonstrates, and more.
  • Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s upcoming film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop.
  • Loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television demonstrates, and more. This time, we take a look at Fjord.

Following in the footsteps of Anatomy of a Fall and Sentimental Value, Cristian Mungiu’s upcoming film Fjord continues a recent trend of complex, critically acclaimed family dramas set against a gorgeous—if appropriately chilly—European backdrop. The Romanian New Wave director won his second Palme d’Or at this year’s Cannes Film Festival for the Norway-set film, which is also his first shot outside of his home country and Romania’s official selection for the best international feature category at the 2027 Oscars.

Loosely based on a real court case, Fjord follows a devout evangelical Romanian man named Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) who move to a remote fjord village in Norway with their five children. Their conservative lifestyle soon puts them at odds with their progressive neighbors, and they find themselves in a custody battle after child abuse allegations surface, setting up a complicated debate between two opposing cultures and worldviews.

Cristian Mungiu’s latest film is based on a real-life court case.

It has been revealed that the film was shot over 36 days in spring 2025 in Western Norway’s Hjørundfjorden. The dramatic and mostly tourist-free fjord near the city of Ålesund cuts through the Sunnmøre Alps, with peaks rising up to 5,600 feet directly from the water.

Industry observers note that for the family home, location scouts selected a tiny village called Stenes, comprising just a few rustic buildings scattered on the shores of the fjord’s Norangsfjorden arm. Nearby, they shot church scenes at a simple wooden structure in the town of Øye with school scenes taking place in Sæbø and courthouse scenes being filmed in the “significant city” of Ålesund.

Industry observers note that as the title of the film suggests, the fjord is more than just a mere setting—it’s a poetic space suffused with symbolic meaning for Mungiu. “I was attracted by this idea of a very secluded community where people can’t avoid finally talking to one another,” Mungiu states. “The fjord evokes for me this need for solidarity among people when confronted with extreme coldness and severe weather.”.

Mungiu sought to balance the epic scale of the fjord setting with the legal drama of the film.

In a recent development, while audiences might expect the grandeur of a fjord to humble the people who live within it, in this movie, Mungiu instead uses the geographical formation to highlight their folly. “Normally, in front of nature’s force, people should become conscious of their fragility,” Mungiu states, “but too often their huge egos make them forget how mortal and insignificant they are, and they end up investing all their energy into imposing their point of view on others.”.

According to recent reports, the landscape worked particularly well within the context of Mungiu’s unique visual storytelling style: He conceives of each scene as a single shot, without cuts or close-ups, letting his characters move through expansive frames. As he describes it, “Every shot needs to be perfectly balanced in terms of light, interpretation, choreography, rhythm.” For this project, he imagined scenes that would call to mind the winter landscapes of Flemish Renaissance master Pieter Bruegel the Elder, who painted small human figures dwarfed by snowy scenery. The wide shots, Mungiu says, “allow the majestic nature to feel a bit intimidating and menacing.”.

The winter landscapes in the film were inspired by the work of Flemish Renaissance painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder.

According to recent reports, when it came time to select the perfect fjord, Mungiu was purely pragmatic. “I imagine scenes quite in detail when I write the screenplay and while scouting,” he explains. “I try to find locations as close as possible to what I’ve imagined.” He drew a “very precise sketch” for his location scout of what he was looking for: two neighboring houses at the end of a fjord, “with mountains and forests behind, quiet deep water in front, and a narrow road connecting them to the rest of the world—all this ideally covered in snow during wintertime.”.

According to recent reports, his production team found a spot that looked just as he envisioned in Stenes, deep down the fjord and away from the coast, to maximize the potential for more snow. Then the hardest part started: convincing the homeowners to rent their properties out for the shoot.

“Once we started our scouting, we felt that we were visiting a form of paradise,” he says. “The light always comes from an angle, the air is pure, the colors are strong, the calm of the ocean is threatening, the snow on the peaks looks menacing.” Everything in the area, he continues, “is clean, organized, precise, logical, and functional.” Mungiu jokes, “For an OCD person like me, it was the perfect place.”.

Of course, the wildness of the fjord came with its own set of challenges, from avalanche warnings to a lack of consistent snow cover (they trucked in powder from the mountains). But Mungiu and his team tried to use these issues to their artistic advantage. On the first day of shooting, for instance, a major storm forced them to move production inside and shoot an emotionally complex scene. Inspired by the dramatic gusts, they hung an enormous Norwegian flag just outside the window to thrash and snap in the gale, “adding a visual element to the inner feelings of Lisbet in a very delicate moment for her as a character.”.

According to recent reports, the primary gateway town for the fjord is Ålesund, a coastal city known for its abundant Art Nouveau architecture. While it’s only about 20 miles from Stenes as the crow flies, the journey takes about two hours of scenic driving and ferry crossings to get to the spots where the movie was shot.

Sebastian Stan as Mihai Gheorghiu, the devout evangelical main character who relocates his family to the titular Norwegian fjord.

If you want to see the fjord for yourself, an ideal lodging option is the lovely Hotel Union Øye, which opened early for the season to host the cast. Now a member of Relais & Châteaux, the gingerbread-like hotel debuted in 1891 and over the decades has hosted the likes of Henrik Ibsen, Arthur Conan Doyle, and Edvard Grieg, who composed music on the piano in the salon.

Sources indicate that it’s also possible to visit Hjørundfjorden on one of Norway’s most iconic journeys: a sailing with Hurtigruten, which is part pleasure cruise line, part local passenger ferry, and part cargo vessel for remote communities. In 2027, the line’s Coastal Express route, which hugs the coast from Bergen in the south to Kirkenes in the north, will visit Hjørundfjorden in May and September, while the Svalbard Line will make a stop at Sæbø in the fjord from May through September. (In the film’s Ålesund-set courtroom scenes, you can even see the ferry looming outside the windows.).

Havila Voyages, a family-run Hurtigruten competitor, also stops in Hjørundfjorden seasonally from September 1 to October 31; optional excursions include a scenic drive through the surrounding countryside and mountain valleys; an e-bike tour through the narrow Norangsdalen valley along the “Queen’s Route” (so named because it was supposedly visited by seven queens); or a guided hike to a mountain dairy farm, followed by a snack of a svele (crepe).

And if you can’t make it to Norway, Mungiu is presenting an exhibition of his photographs from scouting trips and the film’s production called Fjord. The Pictures at Latest York’s Romanian Cultural Institute in New York (through November 30). His images, all shot on a phone, depict the landscapes, people, architecture, and even weather that helped shape the film’s visual language.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes.
  • It has been revealed that since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep.
  • In a recent development, signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

It has been revealed that since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card debuted today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

In a recent development, signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To quell this issue, the fresh card is effectively a build your own card, card.

It has been revealed that despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t….

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
  • Industry observers note that A bill introduced by Sen.
  • Industry observers note that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

Industry observers note that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The latest office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

Sources indicate that “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she remarked in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide remarked.

Sources indicate that the office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

It has been revealed that senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You don’t have to travel to Munich or Nuremberg to get into the Christmas spirit and enjoy some lebkuchen or pfeffernüsse. The streets of the country’s small towns are also filled with holiday cheer that’s best experienced at their Christmas markets. Amid their narrow alleys and on cobblestone squares, there’s a special atmosphere every December. Here’s our selection of seven to visit this season.

The façades of the houses on Bad Tölz’s Marktstraße glow with festive lights in the evening.

According to recent reports, in Bavaria’s Bad Tölz, a medieval town sitting on the Isar River, the scent of roasted almonds mingles with the sound of Christmas carols, while the historic market square is decorated with garlands and wreaths. At the Christmas market, approximately 40 festively decorated stalls are set up right in front of the historic façades of the old town. The atmosphere is especially magical in the evening hours when the Christmas lights sparkle everywhere. For children, there’s a carousel, a curated program of activities, and the popular Family Wednesdays with discounts and carriage rides.

Industry observers note that hours: 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily, from November 27 to December 23, 2026; 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. on December 24.

Recent findings suggest that the Wernigerode Christmas Market is set against the backdrop of some of the historic buildings in this town in the Harz Mountains. Snow often covers the roofs, and Christmas carols fill the air at the popular event.

Hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Friday and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m.; from November 20 to December 22, 2026.

The medieval town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber is even more magical than usual during the Christmas season.

In the pre-Christmas season, the medieval town of Rothenburg ob der Tauber, located on the Romantic Road in Bavaria, becomes even more enchanting. The opening of the market is a small spectacle when, on the Friday before the first Sunday of Advent, the large Christmas tree on the market square is illuminated in a festive ceremony. The town’s Christmas market continues a tradition with more than 500 years of history. In the narrow alleys and squares near the town hall, including the market square, visitors will find everything they could desire as they embrace the Christmas season: from gifts like handmade jewelry to freshly baked gingerbread. The Christmas Village, a nearly 11,000-square-foot store located not far from the Market Square, continues the holiday spirit year-round.

Hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Fridays and Saturdays, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; from November 20 to December 23, 2026, closed November 23.

A special feature of the Gengenbach Advent Market is the window-opening ritual which transforms the town hall into an enormous advent calendar.

According to recent reports, one of the things that makes the Gengenbach Advent Market in the Black Forest stand out is its window-opening ritual. On December 1, the town hall transforms into the world’s largest Advent calendar with a unique art display. Every evening at 6 p.m., one of 24 windows opens. In each one there’s a work of art, often by world-renowned artists such as Marc Chagall and Andy Warhol. Visitors from all over the world come to Gengenbach to see this unique calendar against the romantic backdrop of the historic old town.

Hours: Monday to Friday, 2 p.m. to 8 p.m.; Saturdays and Sundays, 11:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. From November 27 to December 23, 2026.

Quedlinburg is already a World Heritage City, but during the Christmas season it becomes even more romantic.

Hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 8 p.m.; Fridays, 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.; Saturdays, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.. From November 25 to December 22, 2026.

An enchanting setting and a varied program are the draws at the Bernkastel-Kues Christmas Market.

Recent findings suggest that A torch-lit swim, fireworks, and a hike with St. Nicholas: During Advent, the Christmas market in Bernkastel-Kues, a town in a famous winegrowing town near the borders with Luxembourg and Belgium, offers a program of activities that few can match. Torch-lit swimmers bravely plunge into the cold, wintry Moselle on December 5, and both children and adults can join St. Nicholas on a hike on December 6. (The route varies each year, but it always begins at the market square and typically covers between six and nine miles.) This year marks the 48th time the historic old town has served as the backdrop for this romantic Christmas market. Amid half-timbered façades and cobblestone streets, stalls offer traditional crafts, gift ideas, and delicious treats.

Industry observers note that hours: Sunday to Thursday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m.; Fridays and Saturdays, 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. From November 20 to December 20, 2026, closed November 22.

Small and charming, but also very brief: The Meersburg Christmas Market is open for only two days.

Sources indicate that admittedly, a weekend isn’t much time to experience the Christmas market in the old town of Meersburg, on the shores of Lake Constance (Bodensee) in southwestern Germany. But with some carefully planning, you can make the most of the time you have. Both days are packed with Christmas activities, ranging from barrel organ music to readings and puppet shows for the youngest visitors. The stalls sell handicrafts, regional products, and Christmas treats. The market in the castle park is a highlight. And because the event is so short, it makes it all the more special with all the holiday fun concentrated in just two days.

In a recent development, hours: 3 p.m. to 9 p.m., Friday, November 27, and 2 p.m. to 8 p.m., Saturday, November 28, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In a recent development, in 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

In a recent development, the whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic introduced in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

In a recent development, let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following….

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have….

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most newly introduced people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

In a recent development, everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

It has been revealed that the app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

Sources indicate that all the great, major airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

According to recent reports, and in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap organization, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

Industry observers note that my only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

Recent findings suggest that so yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or newly introduced seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a fresh golden age, again.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cayman Airways will launch a new seasonal service to the U.S. next year.

Starting May 21, 2027, the carrier will connect Grand Cayman and Nashville, Tennessee. Flights will operate twice per week, on Mondays and Fridays, through Aug. 16.

Tickets will become available for purchase early next month, officials said.

Cayman Airways is the flag carrier of the Cayman Islands and has its main hub at Owen Roberts International Airport in Grand Cayman.

Its current U.S. destinations are Miami, Tampa, Florida, Austin, Texas, Denver, and Los Angeles.
