    #146848. How We Pulled It Off: A Pakistani Wedding Under the Mudéjar Arches of Seville

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2477 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    How We Pulled It Off: A Pakistani Wedding Under the Mudéjar Arches of Seville

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An incredible love story deserves an incredible wedding.
    • In a recent development, “She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered.
    • Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An incredible love story deserves an incredible wedding. Growing up in the Atlanta suburbs, Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a field trip in middle school, then became best friends as teenagers. It was toward the end of high school that their connection turned romantic.

    In a recent development, “She got into college and was moving out of state, and it felt like this might be the last chance that I would possibly have to be with this girl,” Awaez remembered. “We decided to see where things would take us.”.

    Falaknaz Chranya and Awaez Jiwani met on a middle-school field trip.

    The two grew up in the Atlanta area and got together toward the end of high school.

    Sources indicate that the relationship took them into their twenties through to a proposal in July 2023: an elaborate scavenger hunt that Awaez staged around Chicago, where they lived briefly before turning to Atlanta. When plotting their wedding, they were sure they wanted something just as detailed and thoughtful, and immediately landed on a destination celebration. “We knew we didn’t want to have it in Atlanta, because we didn’t feel like we would be able to give our guests the kind of intentional experience we really wanted to,” notes Falaknaz.

    Ahead, the couple explains how and why they chose to hold a Seville destination wedding in August 2025 for 160 guests, and discusses the (many!) venues they booked for their various events, the fun guest surprise they plotted, and loads of other sangria-soaked details.

    Hotel Alfonso XIII is an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for the Spanish king.

    The property and Sevilla in general are known for the Mudéjar-style architecture of Southern Spain.

    Industry observers note that falaknaz and Awaez were open to getting married anywhere, a wonderful but intimidating prospect. They scoured Pinterest and spoke to planners across the US. “We looked into Chicago, we looked into California, and at one point we looked into a cabin wedding in Montana,” the bride indicates. “None of those really felt right until I came across some of the venues in Seville, Spain.”.

    Her major moment of connection was seeing the Hotel Alfonso XIII, an elegant, historic property commissioned by and named for a king of Spain, who aimed to host esteemed international guests there. The scale and vibe of Seville itself—smaller than other European cities, but with an incredible history, stunning architecture, and loads to do—appealed as well. The couple reached out to several planners and booked a trip to visit the Alfonso and several other venues.

    Sources indicate that in person, the property was just as incredible as they’d hoped. “Hotel Alfonso was honestly a non-negotiable for me once we stayed there that very first trip,” notes Awaez. “We were exposed to all the different ways we could utilize the hotel and make the most of it.”.

    And given the hotel’s 150 rooms, the majority of their guest list could stay there, and did. “One of the major things we wanted from the wedding was everyone to be together. We loved the idea of it being almost a resort, where you’re constantly bumping into people from the wedding,” says Falaknaz.

    The couple chose event-planning firm Bodas del Sur because it had worked on South Asian weddings before.

    Recent findings suggest that as they tried to narrow down the location for their wedding, the couple had a few dismaying calls with potential event firms. “We met with a lot of planners, and they had a lot of stipulations right off the bat. They weren't really open to hearing what we wanted out of our wedding,” Falaknaz says. They ultimately opted to work with Bodas del Sur, a Seville-based firm that specializes in destination weddings across Andalusia and gave them utter confidence in their ideas. “From our very first conversation, they just seemed like they were going to make what we wanted happen,” the bride continues. “Whatever we mentioned, they ran with it, like, ‘Okay, these are all the ways we can make it happen.’ That was the most reassuring thing: that we felt heard.”.

    In addition to their vast experience with Seville venues and vendors, Bodas del Sur had also worked on South Asian weddings in the past, indicates the bride, “so it gave us a lot of confidence that they knew what they were doing.”.

    A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

    Recent findings suggest that A key aspect of the typical South Asian wedding is that it involves several events, and for the couple’s own Muslim-Pakistani celebration, they figured out swiftly that not all of them made sense for the Hotel Alfonso XIII. Though Falaknaz began to panic at the realization—“Of course I was like, all hope is lost, we have to go back to the drawing board”—the Bodas team took them to see more spaces, which cemented Seville for them as a whole.

    Sources indicate that “The first venue they took us to was Casa de Pilatos. We both walked in and were like, ‘Oh my gosh, this is it. We can’t possibly give this up,’” Falaknaz claims. “And the more places they took us to, the more we fell in love with Seville.” The biggest draw for the couple was the city’s rich Islamic heritage—it was under Muslim rule for over 500 years—and the corresponding architectural features, such as the arches, pillars, and intricate tiles, a fusion with Christian motifs known as Mudéjar style.

    A 15th century palace, Casa de Pilatos, played host to the night of dancing and performances known in Packistani-Muslim weddings as the sangeet.

    The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th century formerly private home known for its iconic Sevillian architecture.

    Recent findings suggest that “That blend was something we just weren’t finding elsewhere,” indicates Falaknaz. “That’s truly where we felt like we could give our guests the kind of experience we wanted—that would make them feel connected to something that was more than just a wedding.”.

    The couple held four major events over three days. The mehendi, in which the bride is decorated with henna, was a daytime celebration held at Casa Guardiola, a 19th-century formerly private home commissioned by a nobleman that stands as an apex of Sevillian Romantic architecture. The pithi, another daytime party during which the couple is decorated with turmeric paste to represent a pre-wedding cleansing as well as the golden joy to come, was staged at Hotel Alfonso XIII. The night of dancing and performances, also known as the sangeet, happened at Casa de Pilatos, while the slightly more Western-style wedding reception and its after-party were at Hacienda La Soledad, an estate constructed in 1542 as the center of an olive grove.

    The Sevilla celebration of 160 people felt “tiny” compared to the Atlanta nuptials the couple held for their legal ceremony.

    Recent findings suggest that the one ceremony the couple didn’t have on site in Spain? The actual wedding itself. Their Nikkah, the Islamic wedding rites, was held at an Ismaili Jamatkhana at home in Atlanta, in an effort to include the much larger guest list of everyone important to their families, about 600 people in all. That contributed to the relatively tiny group of 160 in Seville feeling much more intimate—“Well, intimate was still about 160, but intimate for us,” says Falaknaz.

    Recent findings suggest that “We felt connected to doing that in a place where we both grew up. We were able to do it in our mosque at home, the one we grew up going to and where all of our friends and parents’ community is. It was really special to have that be a part of the storyline, that we’ll share hopefully when we have kids,” says Falaknaz. “It was nice to be able to share that with everyone that wouldn't be able to make it to Spain.”.

    The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender cala lilies and pearl chandeliers.

    Given the spectacular aesthetics of their chosen venues, the couple decided to bring in very little outside decor, and keep what they did bring in complementary. “The intention was to find places that spoke for themselves,” says Awaez. “We wouldn’t have to dedicate so much time to constructing the decor, versus the place standing on its own.”.

    For their first two events, they matched the color schemes to the major activities, with the pithi blanketed in shades of turmeric (from fluffy roses to mirrored pillows), and the mehendi outfitted in reddish browns and burnt orange. To create the feeling of intimacy and home at the latter, tables and other furniture were kept low, and wide cushions lay on a floor covered in overlapping rugs to encourage lounging.

    Their sangeet was a night filled with dance performances, channeling a peacock theme to echo the jewel-toned florals and vivid garden colors.

    Industry observers note that their sangeet, the night filled with dance performances, fittingly received a peacock theme, which carried from the feathers embroidered on Falaknaz’s gold gown by Taali to the signage to a jewel-toned palette for the florals. “We pulled colors that we felt would balance the venue, with these beautiful blues in the tiling and obviously the greens in the gardens,” says Falaknaz, who changed into a glittering indigo lehenga by Seema Gujral for her own performance.

    The wedding reception had the simplest decor, in ivory and gold, with tablescapes of singular, slender calla lilies and pearl chandeliers, with architectural floral sculptures set around a fountain. Their planners were the key minds behind the creative vibe of the wedding, along with a local florist, La Galería by Jesús Fuertes.

    Transportation to the sangeet was by horse-drawn carriage, and the couple's photography sessions included a ride around Seville's iconic Plaza de España.

    While the schedule (and culture) of the wedding events was very expected, the couple kept guests on their toes when it came to transportation to the sangeet: They were taken by horse-drawn carriages to Casa de Palatos. “They were so surprised to see a whole bunch of carriages waiting outside for us. It was such a cool moment,” says Awaez. The rides took a scenic route through the Plaza de España before reaching the venue. “We knew that our guests probably weren't going to be able to have a lot of downtime between the events to explore the city,” says Falaknaz of the bonus tour.

    Falaknaz wore a glittering lehenga by Seema Gujral.

    While much of dinner was Desi dishes, the couple also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella.

    It has been revealed that A key part of Awaez and Falaknaz’s three planning trips to Seville involved considering the caterers that their planners suggested. “We were genuinely concerned about how the food was going to taste, especially out in Spain in comparison to our typical Indian-Pakistani restaurants here in the U.S.,” claims Awaez. “We tested and tried a lot of those options that they shared with us, and found several of our own, and ultimately the two that we landed on were fantastic.” They worked with the staff of the Indian restaurant Taj Mahal Sevilla to cater their sangeet, and Ágape 360 Catering y Eventos for their mehendi and reception.

    The gastronomic director of Ágape 360, Manuel de Pablo Deco, is Spanish but was excited to learn and adapt to the couple’s cultural needs: For a few crucial dishes, among them Desi-style karahi paneer and a nihari beef stew, the couple’s mothers actually found YouTube videos demonstrating the technique for cooking the recipes. “We sent those videos over to Manu, and he studied them to a T. He really learned to cook Indian food from scratch,” says the grateful bride.

    It has been revealed that after days of distinctly Pakistani events, the couple’s wedding reception was an unabashed celebration of the local culture. Tinto de verano, a popular summery version of sangria, was served at the cocktail hour, while passed hors d’oeuvres included tapas bites like torta de potatas, Moorish-spiced meat skewers, and chicken croquettes. A troupe of flamenco dancers performed; the couple had seen the group dance at a taverna their planners had recommended on their first planning trip to Seville. While much of their dinner was Desi dishes, they also served the most Spanish of dishes—paella, in both seafood and vegetarian styles—followed by flan for dessert.

    To create the feeling of intimacy, tables and florals were kept low.

    A step and repeat served as a photo op for guests to snap their own shots.

    To maximize their booking and the guest experience alike, Falaknaz and Awaez utilized each possible room or space within their venues. For the sangeet, they took family and couple portraits in the gardens of the Casa de Pilatos, moved to the central, most ornate courtyard for dinner and speeches, held performances in the soaring “courtyard of the halt,” and then moved to an entirely inner room for the after-party, given the local ordinance in the city center that required outdoor spaces to quiet down after 11:00 pm.

    It has been revealed that in order to keep the energy high for that final transition, they enlisted the help of their bridal party, who performed the final dance act of the night. “Almost flash mob style, we ran off the stage and through the crowd and into the indoor space,” indicates Falaknaz. The same crowd-pleasing song that’d been playing outside was already being piped indoors— “Dholi Taro Dhol Baaje,” from the beloved Bollywood movie Hum Dil De Chuke Sanam—so the group of 100+ party-goers was enticed to stay a little longer. Or a lot longer: The party continued back at the hotel’s basement, stretching until 3:00 am.

    The couple invited friends to join them after the wedding for a trip to La Tomatina in Valencia.

    The end of the trip afforded more one-on-one time with guests than the busy wedding weekend.

    In a recent development, wedding events took place Friday through Monday, and most guests left on Tuesday, though plenty decided to extend their trip on either end. The newlyweds themselves decided to attend La Tomatina festival in Valencia, in which festival-goers eat but also pelt each other with tomatoes—otherwise known as the biggest food fight in the world. They threw out an invitation for any interested guests to join them, and more than 30 wound up attending.

    In a recent development, “It was really special to be able to decompress after the wedding with so many of our friends, and actually have more quality time with them than we did at the wedding,” claims Falaknaz. And it turned out to be a suitably colorful ending for an unforgettable wedding celebration.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The cruise world welcomed another giant on Wednesday as MSC Cruises took delivery of one of its largest ships ever, the 216,638-ton MSC World Asia.

    Built at the massive Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire, France, the 20-deck-high, Asia-themed vessel is the third in the line's new World Class series of ships — by far the biggest ships that MSC Cruises has ever built.

    Perhaps more notably, it is the tenth largest cruise ship ever built by any line, smaller only than Royal Caribbean's three Icon Class ships and six Oasis Class ships.

    "Our ambition is simple: To give every guest the best holiday ever," MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago stated Wednesday during a dockside ceremony at the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard to mark the vessel's official handover to MSC Cruises.

    MSC Group is the parent firm of MSC Cruises and sister brand Explora Journeys, a luxury line.

    "We invested in rethinking spaces, developing new concepts and reshaping the experience," Vago added during remarks from a stage set up just in front of the MSC World Asia's bow.

    Vago noted that 60% of the spaces on MSC World Asia are either upcoming or significantly redesigned as compared to the two World Class ships already sailing, MSC World Europa and MSC World America.

    Like those two vessels, MSC World Asia has nearly 2,600 rooms and is capable of holding a whopping 6,758 passengers with every berth filled — more than almost any other passenger vessel afloat.

    It also has similarly massive dimensions with a length of 1,093 feet — the equivalent of nearly four football fields stacked end-to-end — and a width of 154 feet.

    But many of its interior and exterior venues, including a sprawling decktop water park with multiple waterslides and a record-setting dry slide that drops 11 decks, are different from what you'll find on the earlier World Class ships in ways significant and small.

    Related: The terrifying, record-breaking slide on MSC World Asia.

    Among the most significant changes is the addition of latest dining and food concepts, including MSC Cruises' first pan-Asian restaurant and a Venchi chocolate and gelato venue.

    Like the earlier World Class vessels, the ship also offers a sushi bar, teppanyaki restaurant, American-style steakhouse and a branch of the Italian chain Eataly (currently found only on MSC World America), among 20 dining options in all.

    In addition to the water park and dry slide, MSC World Asia's top decks offer multiple pool areas; a suspended-over-the-ocean swing ride called The Cliffhangar; and a ropes course.

    Industry observers note that notable interior features include a three-deck-high dining and entertainment zone called the World Galleria, which is covered by one of the largest LED-lit ceilings at sea. An outdoor extension of this area, called the World Promenade, features more dining and entertainment, plus a new suspended, illuminated Dragon sculpture — part of the ship's Asia theming.

    Related: MSC Cruises cabins and suites guide.

    The arrival of MSC World Asia marks the latest milestone in MSC Cruises' rapid expansion.

    In a recent development, with the addition of MSC World Asia, the brand now operates 24 ships, up from just 13 vessels as recently as 2017. It has nine more on order.

    The ships on the way include five more World Class vessels scheduled for delivery by 2031. Also coming is a upcoming class of four somewhat smaller, 180,000-ton vessels that will be known as the Frontier Class.

    Wednesday's delivery ceremony included a ceremonial lowering of the Chantiers de l'Atlantique and French flags in front of attendees and the raising of the MSC Cruises flag as well as the flag of Malta, where the vessel is registered.

    MSC Group chief financial officer Alexa Aponte Vago, who is married to MSC Group executive chairman Pierfrancesco Vago, served as the traditional "godmother" for the event, which included the smashing of a bottle of Champagne against the ship's hull.

    Joining her husband on stage, Alexa Aponte Vago cut a ceremonial blue ribbon to release the bottle of Champagne against the side of the vessel right on the letter C in its name.

    According to recent reports, while it included a bottle smash, Wednesday's event was not the vessel's official naming. That will take place Saturday in Le Havre, France, at a much larger event.

    MSC World Asia will then head to the Mediterranean, where it will begin its first cruises with paying passengers on Dec. 4 with a voyage out of Barcelona.

    The ship initially will operate seven-night Mediterranean voyages that include stops in France, Italy, Malta and Spain.

    Recent findings suggest that in November 2027, it will reposition to the Southern Caribbean for seven- to 14-night sailings. The itineraries will include stops in Saint Lucia, Grenada, St. Maarten, Antigua and Barbuda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

    Founded in 1861, the Chantiers de l'Atlantique shipyard in St. Nazaire is one of the world's most famous shipyards, known for building many of the world's largest cruise ships as well as naval vessels and wind-powered commercial ships. Notable vessels built at the shipyard include the SS Normandie, SS France, Cunard's Queen Mary 2 and several of Royal Caribbean's Oasis Class ships.

    The shipyard has built 20 vessels for MSC Cruises over the past 25 years.

    It is located at the mouth of the Loire River on the West coast of France.

    Giving Thanks When America Feels Like The Last Days Of Narnia

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, this Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia.
    • Recent findings suggest that in The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned.
    • The deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, this Thanksgiving, I keep thinking about the last days of Narnia. Not because I believe the world is ending, but because C.S. Lewis understood how easily faith can be exploited by those seeking power…and how difficult it becomes to see clearly when we are frightened or angry.

    Recent findings suggest that in The Last Battle, an ape named Shift dresses a donkey in a lion’s skin and persuades the Narnians that Aslan has returned. Shift then speaks for him, demanding obedience and using their love for Aslan to advance his own interests.

    The deception works because the Narnians want to be faithful. They have difficulty believing that someone invoking Aslan could be asking them to betray everything Aslan represents.

    I find that painfully familiar when I watch Christians excuse conduct in Donald Trump that they would rightly condemn in almost anyone else. Once defending a leader becomes a religious obligation, we have given him something that never belonged to him.

    The lion’s skin does not make the donkey Aslan. Invoking Christianity does not make a political demand Christian.

    Industry observers note that that warning applies to me too. Seeing another person’s hypocrisy does not excuse my own contempt. Being right about a political failure does not make every word I write about it righteous.

    Industry observers note that I can become so occupied with what is wrong that I stop noticing what God has given me. I can begin to enjoy indignation. That is a dangerous habit for anyone, particularly someone who writes for a living.

    In a recent development, scripture takes ingratitude seriously. In Romans 1:21, Paul describes people who knew God but neither honored Him as God nor gave thanks. Ingratitude accompanies their descent into darkened thinking and idolatry. And in Ephesians 5:3–4, Paul places thanksgiving where corrupt speech ought to be displaced. Gratitude is part of how we resist sin.

    In a recent development, giving thanks reminds me that I am a recipient of mercy. I have no grounds to treat another person as beyond its reach.

    In a recent development, I remain grateful to be an American. I will continue to criticize our government when I believe it deserves criticism, and I will continue to pray for those who govern us, including President Trump.

    But my allegiance belongs to the Kingdom of Heaven and to Jesus Christ, the King of Kings. No party gets to borrow that allegiance. No president gets to claim it.

    Recent findings suggest that that gives me freedom to acknowledge something good done by someone I oppose and something wrong done by someone I supported. It also means an election cannot deliver everything I hope for or take away everything that matters.

    According to recent reports, paul tells Christians to give thanks in all circumstances (1 Thessalonians 5:18). I understand that to include circumstances I want to change. Gratitude does not require pretending that injustice is good or that incompetence is harmless.

    Today, I am thankful for my wife and children, for the church that has sustained me, my loving and supportive family and friends, and for the extraordinary privilege of traveling through this world and sharing it with you. Most of all, I am thankful that my hope rests with a King whose character does not require excuses.

    Lewis understood that Shift did not have the last word. I need to remember that too.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, united Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Thanksgiving message to thank employees working over the holiday and repeat his conviction that United is the best airline in the world. But his most revealing comment concerned what comes next: he expects United to widen its lead over every other airline.

    In a video filmed at San Francisco International Airport and shared with Live And Let’s Fly, Kirby acknowledged the employees who will spend the holiday taking care of travelers rather than celebrating with their own families.

    He also described hearing regularly from customers about employees who made their journeys easier or did something special for them. That was the most predictable and customary part of a Thanksgiving message, though Kirby could not resist adding a competitive prediction.

    Kirby again called United the best airline in the world, then told employees:.

    “I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines.”.

    That is quite a statement, particularly the reference to all other airlines rather than just American or Delta.

    According to recent reports, I increasingly enjoy flying United. I recently wrote about how Starlink influences which flights I book, and my experiences with the crews and operation have generally been very positive too. Even as a free agent, I find myself drawn back to United. That is a good position for an airline to be in: winning my business because I like the flight it offers rather than because I need another qualifying dollar toward elite status.

    But calling United the best airline in the world remains a much broader claim than I would make. My recent Air France A350 business class flight, for example, offered a level of comfort and dining that United would struggle to match consistently.

    Sources indicate that united also still has a wide variation in its onboard product. An A321neo with Starlink and a comfortable cabin presents a very different experience from an older aircraft with unreliable internet.

    Sources indicate that we can all understand why Kirby speaks this way to employees. He wants them to take pride in the airline and believe that their work is building something better. But the claim becomes more persuasive when passengers can board any aircraft in the fleet and reasonably expect a similarly good experience. That may be coming, but United is still quite a ways off.

    What I appreciated most was Kirby’s emphasis on the individual employees who make travel easier.

    A newly introduced cabin or faster internet can influence which flight I book. The way an employee treats me often determines how I feel about that flight afterward and critically to airlines, whether I would recommend it to others (part of the NPS score).

    That becomes especially apparent when something goes wrong. A delay is frustrating, but an empathetic employee can preserve a lot of goodwill. Being ignored or brushed aside can turn an ordinary disruption into a reason to book another airline next time, which is a frequent matter for me on American Airlines.

    Kirby claims customers tell him about those positive encounters, including on the flight he took that day. It also connects with his recent message after the FAA ground stop, when he highlighted a crew helping a mother traveling with three young children. These are the experiences passengers remember, sometimes long after they have forgotten what they ate or which aircraft operated the flight.

    Sources indicate that happy Thanksgiving everyone! At United, we’re about connecting people and uniting the world and that’s never more true than over the Thanksgiving holiday when we’re about to have our two busiest days of the travel period. I know many of you are going be working hard at the holidays and missing time with your friends and family so I want to say thank you for doing that and really taking care of our customer during this important time.

    As we enter the Thanksgiving holiday, I’m thankful for an awful lot of things in my personal life but in my professional life, I’m thankful for all that you have done in the last several years to make United Airlines the best airline in the world. I fly a lot, including on my flight today, customers constantly are telling me stories about what a flight attendant or a pilot or a gate agent has done to ease their travel to do something special for them that makes a memory for them. So thank you for all you’ve done in the past several years to vault us to a leadership position.

    Thank you for everything you’re doing right now during the holidays to take care of customers and I know we’re going to keep that up in the years to come and the lead that we have is going to grow versus all of the other airlines. Thank you for really doing things to not just make United Airlines the best in the world but to set a new standard for what it means to be a great airline in global aviation. Happy Thanksgiving and thank you.

    Kirby is thankful for the employees who he believes have made United the best airline in the world, and he expects its lead over competitors to grow.

    I share his enthusiasm for much of what United is doing, though I am not ready to award it that title. The more compelling part of his message was the recognition that employees earn customer loyalty through the way they treat people.

    United has given me plenty of reasons to return lately. Continuing to deliver those good experiences will do far more to persuade me than any declaration that it is already the best. To everyone working at the airport or onboard today, thank you. I hope passengers remember that the person helping them get home may be spending the holiday away from their own family.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1313 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    This Cruise Proves the Congo is No Heart of Darkness—Or Viral Fad

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1313 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward.
    • Recent findings suggest that the idea could be stated to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory.
    • Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Occasionally, a place will take hold of our collective imagination in much the same way that an unsolved mathematical problem does, or a treasure hunt, or an ancient, coded message found moldering in an attic, beguiling with its mystery, difficulty, and promise of a reward. Few places exert quite this pull like the Congo Basin, a thick block of forest and rivers covering much of Central Africa, home to some 150 ethnic groups, and a raft of extraordinary biodiversity. Despite its size and its importance as a counterbalance to climate change, the region endures a dearth of scientific research funding and conservation efforts. Roughly the size of India, it has inspired and vexed many visitors (even those who might otherwise have claimed to have conquered it).

    A floating village in the Congo River Basin.

    Recent findings suggest that the idea could be stated to originate in the late 19th century, as Europeans made their way into the great forests seeking fortune and glory. The Welsh explorer Henry Morton Stanley, the first to leave a detailed record of his journey across the Basin, claimed that even after a three-year trek (1874-77) it remained “a region of fable and mystery.” That was exactly the mix sought by Polish sailor Józef Korzeniowski, who, as a boy, looked at the map of Africa, then a white space, and “declared that some day I would go there.” Eventually, and not long after Stanley, he did, and with the captaincy of a steamboat on the Congo River, was tasked with collecting one Mr. Klein, an upcountry agent employed by the brutal Belgian trading tech giant. Korzeniowski was horrified by what he saw along the river—colonization and resource extraction at its cruelest and bloodiest—calling it “the vilest scramble for loot that ever disfigured the history of human conscience and geographical exploration.” Later, Józef Korzeniowski became Joseph Conrad, Mr. Klein became Mr. Kurtz, and the rest is literary history.

    Dzanga Baï, a protected area in the southwestern Central African Republic also known as “the village of elephants.”.

    In a recent development, the latest journeyman to apply themself to the region is another Welshman, Ash Dykes, whose TikTok videos of his journey paddling down the Sangha River (a tributary of the mighty Congo River) have received millions of views. By mid-October, Dykes, who calls himself an extreme athlete, was midway through the 400 miles he hoped to cover. His videos—the anxiety and speculation of his preparation; the amplification of the danger en route—are over-exaggerated, designed to amuse his audience; they are spectacle. Looking bewildered in his state-of-the-art inflatable boat, Dykes is most often met by competent, unaffected locals, paddling their wooden pirogues with balletic grace. And brave though Dykes certainly is, most of what he has accomplished—attending a hunt with the Ba’aka people, seeing the forest elephants in Dzanga Baï, or tracking Western lowland gorillas—can be done by just about anyone.

    The Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions, is the basin's only passenger cruise.

    In a recent development, I, too, was one enchanted by the inscrutability of the Congo Basin, and I dreamt of one day traveling along its rivers and into its forests; in my mind’s eye, I envisioned dusk slipping into night, to the rhythm of a pounding drumbeat. Not long ago, I departed Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, aboard the Princesse Ngalessa, a multi-level riverboat operated by Ducret Expeditions. As the only such passenger vessel in the Congo Basin, the crew of the Ngalessa is accustomed to receiving rarefied looks from the riverbank. But just as often, the ship’s approach was greeted with aplomb, for it was an event in the villages and brought goods, along with community support and news from away.

    In comparison to the coarse and crowded daka-dakas—flat-topped river barges, stuffed with goods and spewing black, acrid smoke as they chunter between Kinshasa and Kisangani—those of us onboard the Ngalessa traveled in glorious comfort: air-conditioning, three square meals a day, and private bathrooms. We also had the benefit of our local guides and their familiarity with the languages, customs, and faces up and down the river. This included, in the riverside village of Ngabe, the appearance of an Ejengi, a forest spirit made of palm fronds that danced and spun as a crowd of onlookers sang, drummed, and screamed in delight.

    “Don’t worry,” our guide mentioned. “Look at his dusty bare feet!” Elsewhere, we watched an Indigenous Luma woman cut, strip, and chew twigs into a pulp that could be used as medicinal pain relief. On other days, we kayaked through the flooded forests of the Alima River, and traded with fishermen who brought their slim pirogues against our mammoth ship to hand over smoked fish and fruit.

    Kayaking through the flooded forests of the Alima River.

    According to recent reports, eight days and 600 miles after leaving Brazzaville, we arrived at the outpost of Ouesso on the Sangha River. I journeyed further upon that water by launch boat, into the Central African Republic, and spent days at Sangha Lodge, drinking gin and tonics with local legend Rod Cassidy, an eco-tourism pioneer who has spent years living and working with the local Ba’aka people. It was through him I had the good luck to attend a hunt with those same Ba’aka, and to look on while they divvied up the duiker they snagged in their homemade nets. Afterwards, they whooped and hollered as they carried the meat out and into their village—a feast!

    In the heightened state of travel, there comes occasionally a moment like falling into an empty space and, as two glancing stones can spark a blaze, a light of comprehension is illuminated. Sometimes this moment manifests itself as love, other times as admiration, or confusion. Conrad left the Congo in spiritual, psychological, and physical shock. “Before the Congo, I was a mere animal,” he wrote after his consequential journey. He was changed, as travelers who go forward with their ears and eyes open (to say nothing of their hearts) are changed. Watching the Ba’aka poised in their hunt, ears tilted to the slightest sound, I felt myself see humanity as it had existed since time immemorial. As they laughed and chatted on their success, the women showing their fangs (chipped with rocks as a show of strength), and the men slapping each other on the back, I could barely remember seeing such happiness elsewhere.

    Recent findings suggest that the Congo Basin may still be raw and atavistic—great adventures there are still possible—but it is no “heart of darkness” (a title which for Conrad lay not in the location itself, but rather mankind’s ability to exploit and vilify others). What separates it from other places is its independence. It requires protection, yes, but has no need, and few provisions, for any prying visitors; it is not a prize to be conquered. Most incredibly, it remains the home of peoples who have not yet latched themselves to tourism; people who sustain themselves almost wholly from an expanse of forest and the waters that for others can only be the basis of wonder and amazement. And yet, after all the sorrow and misery that colonialism brought to the Congo Basin, the people remain sincere and earnest, and willing to show others the best of their land.

    A lone kayaker glides underneath a hazy sky.

    One night, as the Ngalessa drifted northward, from beneath the awning on the ship’s upper deck, I watched a cloud bank clump and darken. Finally, with an incision of lightning, the downpour came, brief but fierce. The sun returned, low in the sky but still warm, and the scent of damp earth rose up. A patter of drumming reached us from somewhere, before being swallowed by the forest. The dinner bell rang, and I thought I never want this trip to end.

    A Thanksgiving Resolution

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Liveandletsfly

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The boy grew into a man and his eyes were opened to the world around him, to the beauty of nature, the sights and smells of the world’s great cities, and the elegance of the human race.
    • Humanity, for all its hints of goodness, was inimitably at war with itself.
    • The man took this all in, wondering where his place was in all this was.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The boy grew into a man and his eyes were opened to the world around him, to the beauty of nature, the sights and smells of the world’s great cities, and the elegance of the human race. But he noticed something else, something troubling.

    Humanity, for all its hints of goodness, was inimitably at war with itself. Not just wars of weaponry and nation states, but deeper wars of ideas and values. Like a cancer imperfectly treated, the pestilence of irreconcilable division ebbed and flowed…but perpetually manifested itself in fierce battles and spilled blood.

    The man took this all in, wondering where his place was in all this was. A humanitarian? A missionary? A soldier? A politician? A writer? A peacemaker? Perhaps a little of each. Perhaps none of the above. He married a woman from a different culture and with a different worldview. The challenge of marriage personified the challenge of the surrounding world — putting differences asides to build trust, loyalty, and respect while growing in love and patience. Was this even possible absent divine intervention?

    According to recent reports, then one Thanksgiving Day it hit him. He could not change the world. Not alone anyway. But there was one one thing he could do, something so trite on the one hand but absolutely revolutionary on the other: he could love his neighbor as he loved himself.

    According to recent reports, just how would that look? Being honest, generous, forgiving, joyful, peaceful, patient, kind, and faithful to everyone he encountered. He would often fail, but it became a primary goal in life.

    The man still ponders his place in this world, but there is one thing he knows — there may be many things he is not, but he is a traveler and that gives him a unique opportunity to put his maxim to practice in venues far beyond the friendly confines of home. Blessed with so much through circumstance of birth, he pauses to reflect upon the blessings he has been the recipient of, many from those who follow a similar maxim.

    Perhaps one day you will meet him and he can encourage you or share in your struggles. His goal is to leave every person he crosses paths with knowing that they are loved and respected. Life is often unkind and this goal is insurmountable in all places and at all times, but it is worth pursuing.

    Industry observers note that now, he invites you to join him in his journey to put others before himself. One day and one person at a time, humanity can tame the inhumane world it finds itself in.

    This post has appeared annually on Thanksgiving Day since 2015.

    Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S.
    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    Recent findings suggest that trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    In a recent development, “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    Sources indicate that his interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    Sources indicate that both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    Industry observers note that “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump said as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    Industry observers note that “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Newly introduced York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump noted, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    Industry observers note that other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of concerns, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer noted.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He remarked it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers noted they doubted very much would come from it.

    In a recent development, “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal noted Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    Industry observers note that on spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to swiftly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

    A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.

    Recent findings suggest that the airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian. Deliveries are expected from 2031 to 2034.

    Sources indicate that the deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

    President Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

    Recent findings suggest that trump said earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

    Sources indicate that china Southern mentioned the new aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.

    #146836. Tech Report: The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1100 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: The 11 Most Beautiful Beaches in the Caribbean

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs.
    • Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here.
    • In a recent development, grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, picking the most beautiful beaches in the Caribbean is an exercise in splitting hairs. Nearly every island has a stretch of powdery sand and improbably blue water, and after a while, the “nice sand, nice water” trope stops registering at all. We’re talking beauty in the transcendental sense—the kind of beauty that makes you feel something. Maybe it’s a crescent of sand more pink than you thought could happen in nature. Maybe it’s a labyrinth of granite boulders spilling into the sea. Or maybe it’s a beach bar so perfectly placed it feels as much a part of the landscape as the sand. Plenty of beaches are picturesque. These are the ones, if you ask us, that are beautiful.

    Barbuda is the quieter, more elusive sister to Antigua, but Princess Diana Beach is the reason many visitors make a detour here. The long stretch of blush-pink sand is framed by low vegetation and blissfully few signs of life. There is, almost puzzlingly, a Nobu, which brings a welcome blip of civilization in the form of Japanese-Peruvian cooking, cocktails, and a beach club with cabanas. (Nobu Beach Inn is set to debut in 2027, too.) Book lunch there and a beach transfer in advance—many of the top resorts on Antigua offer this as a day excursion from the other island.

    In a recent development, grace Bay is famous for good reason: roughly three miles of powdery white sand and shockingly clear waters make even the most airbrushed postcards look inadequate. An offshore reef keeps the waters agreeably calm for swimming (especially with kids), too. This is one of the Caribbean’s most polished beach destinations, with a concentration of luxury resorts, watersports operators and restaurants that make a choose-your-own adventure beach day a pretty seamless affair. Public access points are plentiful and free, so you needn’t be staying at one of the grand hotels to enjoy the view. (Although you should.).

    Recent findings suggest that the kind of place that castaway dreams are made of, Little Bay is a tiny crescent of sand tucked beneath towering limestone cliffs. No beach club, no cabanas, no infrastructure, no fuss. It’s accessible by boat from neighboring Crocus Bay, or, if you’re feeling adventurous, by rope down the rock face. Bring water, a picnic and all your gear—there’s fantastic snorkeling here.

    Industry observers note that A mile-long horseshoe of white sand with clear, shallow water, Flamenco Beach is more than worth the ferry over from mainland Puerto Rico. It also has an unusual bit of history: two abandoned United States military tanks, left behind after the Navy used Culebra for training exercises, now sit near the shore, covered in colorful graffiti. We aren’t usually proponents of littering, but the counterpoint of natural beauty with human history is part of what makes this beach so unforgettable.

    Industry observers note that definitely the most photographed beach in the U.S. Virgin Islands and probably the most photographed beach in the Caribbean, Trunk Bay never disappoints. From the access road, you see a sweep of white sand stretching out, with impossibly turquoise waters and a small offshore cay that seems placed for composition. It’s part of Virgin Islands National Park, so the infrastructure covers all the stuff you need—snack bar, restrooms, showers and snorkel rentals. The main attraction is the underwater snorkeling trail, where submerged markers introduce visitors to the coral reef and its inhabitants.

    If you want swanky French beach clubs, head over to Saint-Jean, because Saline is St. Barth’s at its most elemental. The sand is broad and soft, the dunes rolling, and the sea open, with no beach clubs or hotels or influencers interrupting your view. Getting there requires a short walk over the dunes from the parking lot, which helps preserve the feeling that you’re leaving the chi-chi side of the island behind.

    There are beautiful beaches, and then there are the Baths, a landscape so distinctive it feels like you’ve left the Caribbean, and perhaps earth entirely. The beach is home to a collection of enormous granite boulders, some as large as houses, all tumbled together to create something totally unique. Between them are hidden grottoes, tidal pools and narrow passages—making this as much a playground as it is a beach. Bring sturdy water shoes and expect to do some scrambling.

    Recent findings suggest that the longest beach on its island, this elegant crescent sits directly on the Tropic of Cancer. It’s relatively remote and unspoiled by Bahamian standards, making it a true bucket list destination for beach snobs. It’s about a 30-minute drive from George Town on Great Exuma (where the airport is), across the bridge to Little Exuma. There are no proper facilities, so pack what you need. There are Aman, Rosewood and Bulgari resorts debuting here in the years to come—so visit now for serious “I've been coming here since” bragging rights.

    A hidden gem by any standard, Sandy Island is a miniature, uninhabited coral cay located just off the west coast of Carriacou, Grenada’s sister island. There are no hotels or roads, and the whole appeal is the rugged simplicity of arriving by boat, dropping anchor and spending an afternoon doing basically nothing except enjoying the elements. The island is part of a protected marine park, making it a fantastic spot for snorkeling with colorful reef fish, turtles and octopi.

    Sources indicate that the rest of the world is finally catching up with what the diving scene has known for years—No Name Beach is one of the most pristine, stunning stretches of sand anywhere in the Caribbean. It’s located on the tiny island of Klein Bonaire (“Little Bonaire”) just offshore of mainland Bonaire, and is part of Bonaire National Marine Park, meaning development is off the table. There aren’t any restaurants, bathrooms, or beach bars, but there are water taxis from Kralendijk. Bring food and water, your own snorkel gear, and prepare to be blown away by the untouched Caribbean at its finest.

    While Bávaro Beach proper is about 5 miles long, it connects seamlessly with adjoining beaches Arena Blanca and Arena Gorda—so, depending on who’s counting, actually comes in at closer to 30 miles of uninterrupted shoreline. This is the beach that initially spurred Punta Cana’s resort boom, with coconut palms fringing the white sand, a barrier reef keeping the waters tranquil, and enough space for everyone to stretch out and (pretty much) never feel crowded. If you head toward El Cortecito or Los Corales, you’ll find beach bars where the party never stops. On a beach this beautiful, why would it?

    #146834. Breaking: How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1490 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: How a Screen-Free Retreat in South Africa’s Cederberg Rewired My Nervous System

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1490 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater.
    • My phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres.
    • Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As the sun dropped behind craggy peaks, the heat-baked sandstone dissolved into a deep twilight, and the silence thickened until the valley became a dark amphitheater. I had come to Bliss & Stars, an off-grid retreat perched above the Doring River deep in South Africa's Cederberg, for Orion's Odyssey, a program timed to the newly introduced moon, when the sky is at its darkest. As we neared midnight, the Milky Way's galactic core rose above the ridge, so dense and richly textured, it looked like the luminous, flowing reflection of the river below.

    My phone had lost signal hours earlier, somewhere on the winding, vertiginous drive into this private reserve of over 3,300 acres. Initially, I had found that confronting, until I made peace with what I stood to gain. The eye needs around 20 minutes of true darkness to adjust, and a single glance at a bright screen largely undoes it. Without a signal, I had no reason to look down at it. It was just a camera.

    Cradled by ancient rock, Weaver’s Nest is a villa for two above the Doring River.

    According to recent reports, that encompassing darkness is what brought Heine Rasmussen, an astronomy and nature guide and science communicator, and his wife Daria, a meditation teacher and somatic practitioner, here. In 2018, they left behind the security of corporate life in Copenhagen for a quest to find the least light-polluted skies. After searching around the world, they found them in the Cederberg, just over four hours north of Cape Town.

    Sources indicate that they acquired the virtually untouched land in 2019, and first had to construct a rudimentary access road before they could start building the lodge. Everything came in by pickup truck and trailer, and was carried by hand for the last stretch. The chalets were wedged between boulders or into the rock face above the river. More recently, the couple added a villa, bringing the total to six units that can accomodate no more than 10 guests.

    On these monthly, stargazing-centered retreats, the nights belong to Heine. After dinner each evening, we gathered on a circular, open-air viewing deck in front of the observatory, where mattresses were laid out so we could lie flat and look straight up. One night Heine led us on what he calls "a little mental space walk," a star meditation designed to unground rather than ground us, during which he recounted the history of the universe. With our eyes closed, we breathed the night in through the nose and out through the mouth while he invited the city's stress to leave with each exhalation, until gravity seemed to loosen its grip and our arms and legs felt as if they might float. Falling asleep, he assured us, was perfectly fine.

    After a night of stargazing, morning breathwork and yoga with Daria help put life into perspective.

    The Cederberg's sandstone boulders have been sculpted by wind and water over aeons.

    Industry observers note that at the 20-inch telescope, one of the largest privately owned in South Africa, he taught us without jargon, finding a nebula and talking our small group through it while we took turns peering into the eyepiece. Guests here range from billionaires seeking quiet to people who come for free on the lodge's bursary program, and all of them arrive curious, looking for purpose, or simply to disconnect from the world they’ve left behind.

    Heine's first subject: time. Moonlight, he told us, reaches us about a second after leaving the moon; sunlight about eight minutes after leaving the sun. The two pale patches in the southern sky, the Magellanic Clouds, are satellite galaxies of our own, and their light set out more than 160,000 years ago, when our species was young and still almost entirely in Africa. From there he moved to the iron in our blood and the calcium in our bones, forged in stars that exploded before our sun ever existed. I had heard the stardust line many times in other remote locales but never within the context of physics, explained step by step, or woven into a meditation under a sky like this one.

    Daria took care of the mornings, which began with a thick, warm ceremonial cacao, readying the nervous system for what was to follow. I missed my regular wake-up coffee, the richness of the chocolatey cacao not compensating for the familiar kick of caffeine. From there, we headed to our yoga mats in an open-air studio where Daria led us in somatic breathwork, referencing the enormity of the night sky. Her view is that star-studded skies like those the Cederberg reliably delivers do not make daily concerns disappear; they merely change their size, put them into perspective. Much of what she imparts during the morning breathwork sessions is about making room to allow yourself to feel that. Daria works with the stress the body becomes so good at absorbing—shallow breaths and a clenched jaw, in my case. From hysterical laughter to sobs of grief, more surfaced for our small circle than any of us had bargained for.

    The Cederberg has some of the darkest skies on earth.

    After brunch, we hiked narrow paths where Cape mountain leopard tracks were pressed into the sand and raptors like Verreaux's eagles and rock kestrels caught thermals overhead. We scrambled over the orange sandstone rock, carved into fantastical shapes piled like giant, irregular building blocks, before washing off the dust and dry heat in the Doring River, the water surprisingly cool even though it was the end of summer. In the overhangs we marveled at San rock paintings between 2,000 and 5,000 years old, a collection of sites which Heine and Daria are still discovering on their land. There are more than 2,500 known rock art sites in the wider Cederberg, and whenever I see them I can't help thinking that the people who left their mark here once stood in this same silence, under much the same stars.

    Every plant-based meal is consciously plated to nourish body, mind, and spirit.

    According to recent reports, with so much of the day spent on the move, in silence or alone, meals at the long wooden table in the lodge's open-blueprint kitchen became the social high point. With caffeine, refined sugar, meat, and alcohol off the menu, dining still felt indulgent despite being based on vegetables, fruit, and whole grains. Daria has little patience for the guilt and pressure so often associated with clean-eating dogma; in the retreat's cookbook, Eat, Thrive, Repeat, she writes about reaching the point where "appetite becomes information rather than judgment." In practice, that meant buddha bowls, ancient grain salads, roasted vegetables, and sweet treats at brunch like beetroot flapjacks with a miso caramel of dates and coconut oil.

    Sources indicate that one night, after hiking into the sunset and a surprise dinner in a cave, Heine gave an informal introduction to one of his passions, astrophotography. I learned how to hold a shutter open long enough to gather light the eye cannot. I stood still in the pitch black with a torch under my chin and came away with a portrait of myself against thousands of stars, the camera collecting photons that had been traveling for centuries, some for millennia, before they reached its sensor.

    As you fall asleep, the night sky is framed in floor-to-ceiling glass.

    Industry observers note that on the final night, the telescope and the table worked in tandem. Dinner with Stars ran to six courses, eaten between turns at the eyepiece, and, read in order, the menu told the life story of the universe much as Heine had been telling it to us since we arrived—from Big Bang, a baked carrot dish, through to The White Dwarf, a wild strawberry dessert named for the small, dense ember a star like our sun leaves behind when it dies. The carbon on my fork was made inside stars that died before our sun existed, scattered into space, swept into the cloud of gas and dust that became our solar system, and pulled from the air, eventually, by the carrots on my plate.

    Because it was summer and we had to wait for the sky to turn inky black, nights ended well past midnight. Back in my chalet, on a bed stuffed with horsehair, seaweed, and coconut fiber, I sipped from a flask filled with locally grown rooibos sweetened with wildflower honey before drifting off to sleep. The chalet's floor-to-ceiling windows face east over the river and are free of curtains to encourage waking with the morning light—a gentle but powerful way to reset one's circadian rhythm. When I opened my eyes in the small hours, the night sky filled the glass. I had never seen it framed like that.

    Running year-round except July in South Africa's Cederberg, Bliss & Stars hosts intimate, all-inclusive retreats in six off-grid units sleeping a maximum of 10 guests.

    The House has a upcoming lame-duck challenge: Attendance

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a latest challenge: Attendance.
    • Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, mentioned attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a latest challenge: Attendance.

    Thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-highlights – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    The House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    In a recent development, "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    Of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    Johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    Industry observers note that “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, said. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    According to recent reports, “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    According to recent reports, “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan said. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    Recent findings suggest that attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    Industry observers note that “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., said. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

Their signature Afternoon Tea service will also be available from 11:30 am to 4:00 pm on Christmas.

    According to recent reports, what’s more festive than tucking into a fancy steak dinner on Christmas? Pair any of them with a dry-aged tomahawk ribsteak and 28-Day dry-aged porterhouse served with tableside truffle service.

    If you’re looking for Christmas dinner to enjoy with a group, Limusina’s menu of coastal Mexican-inspired fare is especially shareable; think Serrano Guacamole, Flamed Queso Fundido and a rotating selection of seasonal plates prepared over live fire. The holiday cocktail menu includes the Après Ski Sangria, featuring red wine, mulling spices and winter citrus; Home Alone, with bourbon, cinnamon and house spruce bitters; and Quality Nog, blending Bacardi Ocho, Cognac and a delightful homemade spiced nog.

Rooted in the vibrant and inclusive spirit of Harlem, Red Rooster Harlem is inspired by the neighborhood’s African American, Southern, and Caribbean culinary influences with exciting dishes like its signature Yardbird fried chicken, cornbread and gravy, shrimp and grits, oxtail meatloaf, and more.

    At Le Crocodile, the cozy French bistro inside Williamsburg’s Wythe Hotel, celebrate Christmas Day with a special prix fixe menu. Dessert options include Mont Blanc with Biscoff & Cranberry. Afterwards, head upstairs for a cocktail at Bar Blondeau, and enjoy sweeping views of a (quieter) city.

The beverage program features playful takes on South Indian classics, including the dosa martini, made with Jamun gin, St. Germain, and Lillet Blanc, and the palm paradise (coconut kallu, curry leaves, lychee cordial, and lemon cordial).

For dinner, the menu features nizami keema (ground lamb with cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, and lemon zest), paneer pasanda (fresh cheese in a rich cashew-onion sauce), and Achari Hiran Ki Chhampen (venison chops marinated in hung yogurt, pickling spices, and roasted chickpea flour).

    Recent findings suggest that one of the few restaurants in the city open for Christmas lunch as well as dinner, Indian fine dining destination Musaafer is serving up its crowd-favorite paneer tikka, eponymous daal Musaafer, coriander shrimp, and more. The highlight of the menu is a festive plum cake layered with black pepper and Old Monk rum crémeux, cranberry compote, and sudachi lime gelée, topped with delicate makhan malai (milk cream). It’s finished with almond-sugar snowflakes, gold and silver pearls, and a dusting of snow sugar.

    According to recent reports, why not ring in the holiday with creations from one of the city’s best pastry chefs? At Lysée, chef Eunji Lee offers a seven-course ($130 per person) dessert tasting menu of savory and sweet pastries; menu highlights include Lysée’s signature Black truffle ice cream cone, made with black truffle ice cream and a slice of chocolate waffle cone and chocolate caramel, a Mont Blanc with cognac ice cream, a mini mushroom quiche, an Ossetra caviar tart, and more. Choose from four two-hour seatings available at 11:30 AM, 1:30 PM, 3:30 PM, and 5:30 PM, with an optional wine pairing.
