    According to recent reports, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    In a statement McIver remarked she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver stated in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    According to recent reports, the criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    Industry observers note that court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    In a recent development, earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    Finding Unexpected Kinship With Senior Travelers—And a Joyful Latest Outlook On Growing Older

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.
    • According to recent reports, on my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that on a grassy field in Don-Aryk, Kyrgyzstan, men on horseback were wrestling over a headless goat carcass. This is kok boru, the country's national sport, sometimes called dead goat polo. The riders violently wrenched the goat from one another's grip, then tore across the field toward a cauldron-size goal. When the game ended, a player invited me to take a victory lap with the goat. I was two weeks into a Smithsonian Journeys trip across five Central Asian countries with a group of mostly retirees. They knew I was genuinely considering his offer, and their reaction was unanimous: Oh, no you won't.

    Standing there in the Kyrgyz countryside, being collectively talked out of one of my more impulsive yeses by a busload of surrogate parents, I felt like a teenager being scolded—defiant but also secretly touched that people I had just met cared enough to save me from myself.

    According to recent reports, on my first trip to Uzbekistan, I joined an Intrepid Travel tour and wondered whether I had booked the wrong departure. Most of the guests were seniors, so I assumed we would have little in common. Then I met Penny, a septuagenarian from Australia who survived a terrorist bombing in Bali that killed three people in her group. Her husband had suffered brain damage and withdrew from the world; Penny kept traveling, even when it meant going alone. We shopped for textiles in Khiva and bonded over meals; by trip's end, whatever distance I'd imagined between us disappeared.

    Sources indicate that that first trip changed more than my assumptions about whom I might enjoy traveling with. My own parents struggled with severe depression and agoraphobia, each condition feeding the other as their shared world contracted. Older travelers like Penny showed me another way to age: by staying curious, social, active, and engaged with the world.

    Industry observers note that I saw that same determination on a Lindblad Expeditions–National Geographic cruise through the Peruvian Amazon. Dan and Kathy, both widowed after 30-year marriages, met online, fell in love, and kept a list of trips to take. Another guest had cared for her husband through terminal brain cancer, then received her own cancer diagnosis. Hardship hadn't blunted their zest for adventure; if anything, it had magnified it.

    I was on board and turning that contrast over in my mind when I found out my dad died.

    The next few days bled together. Through the blur my fellow travelers indicated up for me—listening when I wanted to talk and giving me space when I didn't. These folks knew firsthand what it meant to have life cleaved into Before and After. Yet here they were, swimming with piranhas, trekking through the jungle, and plotting where to go next. They were living proof that joy could still exist on the other side of tragedy.

    Back in Central Asia my fellow travelers who had vetoed my kok boru ride embodied what I'd come to love about traveling with groups of older people. Linda, an 80-year-old retired psychoanalyst, shared my raunchy humor and skittering attention span during tedious museum tours. I suspected Susan, 83, disapproved when she first asked about my tattoos—until she rolled up her sleeve to reveal Betty Boop on her biceps, acquired at 81. She had survived two comas and a stroke, and still posed for photos in fire-engine red lipstick. A red lip is my signature too. This was my kind of woman.

    Sources indicate that the whole group was intimidatingly accomplished: pulmonologists, oncologists, former heads of ICUs and surgical departments. Ask for a doctor, and half the bus could raise a hand. They talked passionately about history and architecture. My PhD dad could turn any conversation into a lecture too; I hadn't realized how much I missed that until I was sermonized at dinner. Their adult children came up often: Would they find the right partner? Start a family? Live up to their potential? Beneath all the second-guessing was enormous tenderness.

    Traveling with seniors requires patience, of course. Some use canes and walkers, so itineraries are deliberately less demanding. To me, that's a fair trade.

    On a Viking river cruise that sailed this past summer from Bucharest, Romania, to Budapest, my husband and I hit it off with Bob and Jeannie, a couple from Long Island. They peppered us with questions about our work, our four-year-old son, and our life in Minnesota. That curiosity touched a nerve. My mother, who has dementia and lives with us, no longer asks about my job, my kid, or anything else. Soon we were seeking one another out, talking for hours and doubling over with laughter. We promised to look them up the next time we were in Upcoming York—and meant it. Bob and Jeannie weren't filling in for anyone. They were just friends.

    At our farewell Smithsonian dinner in Almaty, the group toasted me for “keeping us young.” I was usually the one volunteering to dance with strangers, climb onto horses, or let an owl perch on my head. If I got parental supervision in return, they got to live vicariously through my harebrained antics.

    Recent findings suggest that their gratitude caught me off guard. I knew what these travelers gave me—perspective, attention, a road map for the years ahead—but hadn't considered what I might be giving them.

    According to recent reports, now, when I join a group trip, I genuinely hope I'm the youngest person on the bus. I look forward to seeing whom I'll connect with, hearing stories I'll carry for years, and, if I'm lucky, getting a glimpse of the person I might become.

    Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across Upcoming Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

    Utah-based Breeze Airways has carved out a niche for nonstop flights in secondary markets across the US. The low-cost carrier offers a unique point-to-point market on underserved domestic routes and operates a fleet of modern Airbus A220-300s.

    Reviewing data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) suggests that a number of its routes are flying below the 'sweet spot' of 80% load factor. This is a target most airlines set to ensure that all operational costs are covered and that the route turns a profit. Overall, the average Breeze load factor sits at 77.9%.

    Despite Breeze's rapid expansion across the US since the airline's launch in 2021, the airline's primary focus has been connecting secondary cities with nonstop flights. Reviewing the data from BTS, it suggests the airline's poorest performing routes flew with an average of less than 46% during the period of January to August 2026.

    These low numbers are the polar opposite to the airline's fullest routes, which average more than 91% load factor, with the most popular route for the airline being that of Atlantic City (ACY) to Orlando (MCO), achieving a 93.8% average load factor.

    As a comparison, the poorest performing route was between Orange County (SNA) and Montrose (MTJ), which averaged load factors of just 22.4%, which forced the carrier to suspend the service in April of this year.

    Average Load Factor (Between January and August 2026).

    Sources indicate that with Orange County and Montrose having the poorest load factors, which led to the route being suspended, a number of other routes in the Breeze network are still performing with low patronage, questioning whether the airline may reconsider these routes. Simple Flying reached out to Breeze for comment on the below routes' load factors; however, an airline spokesperson could not immediately be reached.

    For Breeze, its second-worst-performing route is between Charleston (CHS) in South Carolina and Richmond (RIC) in Virginia. The route continues to operate, despite a load factor averaging 38.5%. This is followed by Louisville (SDF) and Pittsburgh (PIT), which began in April and have only been able to achieve a 42.8% load factor. This route is expected to end in January.

    Sources indicate that flights from Washington Dulles (IAD) nonstop to Ogdensburg (OGS) in upstate New York are another route that was forced to end due to load factors, with Breeze operating at just 45.6%. Full details of the airline's poorest-performing routes are in the table below:.

    Airlines will typically aim for an 80% passenger load factor, to cover high fixed costs and historically thin profit margins. Aiming for 80% helps cover the operating costs and turns the flight profitable. This can fluctuate between airlines, but this is the industry benchmark.

    After Atlantic City to Orlando remains the airline's most popular route by load factor, the carrier's transcontinental services continue to pull high patronage. The airline's second most popular route is that of Norfolk (ORF) to San Diego (SAN), which during the period of January to August of this year recorded a 93% load factor.

    Los Angeles (LAX) to Richmond is another popular link, which during the same period achieved 92.3% load factor.     #146825. How to Spend Christmas in Paris

    📅 14 Dec 2017 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2371 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Spend Christmas in Paris

    📅 14 Dec 2017 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2371 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper.
    • Oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them.
    • Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Strasbourg may be France’s holiday capital, claiming the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but there’s no denying Christmas in Paris is a showstopper. The city shines brighter each year with thousands of lights illuminating its famous squares and landmarks like the Champs-Elysées, dubbed the “world’s most beautiful avenue.” Holiday cheer seeps into each of the 20 arrondissements, decorated with larger-than-life garlands, forests of bauble-strewn fir trees, sculptural light displays, and wooden chalets doling out vin chaud (mulled wine) and holiday specialties like foie gras—best spread on subtly sweet pain d’épices (gingerbread).

    Oyster stands are as much a fixture of the holidays in Paris as Christmas markets—which happen to be one of the best places to try them. Fête the season in true French fashion with a movable feast dining and drinking at some of the city’s most iconic institutions, from Left Bank cafés where famous writers and artists once gathered to the Palace hotels huddled around Place de la Concorde and Place Vendôme. And when you’re ready to indulge in Paris’s renowned retail therapy, swing by one of the grand magasins (department stores), which rank among the best in the world for their holiday window displays—Fresh York City included—executed with the same style and precision as a couturier. The city may not be blanketed in snow, but the holiday spirit is as strong here as on the slopes in the French Alps—and even has the cuisine and chalets to prove it. If you’re planning to spend Christmas in Paris, you’ll find plenty of ways to celebrate, but these nine are some of the best things to do and see during the holidays in the City of Light.

    Read our complete Paris travel guide here, which includes:.

    Every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that activity. When choosing things to do, our editors consider landmarks and experiences that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with upcoming information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Lindsey Tramuta.

    Sources indicate that this winter, Oscar winner Cate Blanchett will lead the lighting ceremony of the 2 million LED lights illuminating the Champs-Elysées, running all the way up to the Arc de Triomphe. Sparkling each evening from 5:00 pm to 1:00 am, the most iconic avenue in Paris and its 400 balloon glass garland-adorned trees are coordinating with another famous landmark—the Eiffel Tower—twinkling in unison on the hour. Every quarter of an hour, the Champs-Elysées will put on a light show set to Vivaldi’s Four Seasons, and on December 24 and 25, the avenue will glow in Christmas-themed green and red. As part of the Fresh Year’s Eve countdown to midnight under the Arc de Triomphe, when a music-themed fireworks show will ring in 2027, the lights will shine in a tricolor blue, white and red display running down the avenue. Making a grand return after a decade-long pause, a Christmas market will run from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe with more than 200 stalls and an ice rink near the Pavillon Ledoyen.

    It has been revealed that dining with a view takes on a whole upcoming meaning as you settle in by the panoramic windows on Ducasse sur Seine, the sole electric boat cruising the river. The floating restaurant is as gastronomic an experience as anything on land thanks to Alain Ducasse, the namesake chef behind the modern Parisian cuisine who claims a record-setting number of coveted Michelin stars. With chef Jean-Philippe Berens and the team prepping everything fresh on board, you’ll have prime views of the Seine while dining in style on Christmas Eve during the six-course menu, which features everything from silky foie gras royale to raw scallops topped with gelée and caviar—plus a cheese course with 18-month-matured truffled Comté.

    Sources indicate that the ambiance is equally as elegant at Ducasse Baccarat, where the chef’s cuisine is presented in an opulent space dripping in chandeliers and tableware designed by the French fine crystal creator. One of the few spots open daily during the holiday season, the restaurant ups the ante on Christmas Eve and Latest Year’s Eve with themed degustation menus.

    Recent findings suggest that france’s Capital of Christmas, Strasbourg, is home to the country’s oldest Marché de Noël, but Paris is dotted with more than a dozen markets and Christmas villages—the largest being La Magie de Noël in the Tuileries Garden, stretching from the Louvre to Place de la Concorde, which remains open until early January. There, you’ll discover hundreds of wooden cabins selling small gifts and seasonal treats; a selection of stands run by French artisans, from glassblowers to woodworkers; and attractions like a small ice rink and carnival rides—the Ferris wheel being the highlight, especially during the Eiffel Tower’s hourly light show.

    In a recent development, on the Square René Viviani, directly across from Notre Dame, you’ll find an intimate market with some 30 exhibitors selling regional food, hot chocolate, and handmade crafts. On the Left Bank, the Saint-Germain-des-Prés Marché de Noël unfolds along the namesake boulevard, next to the church, with wooden chalets and gourmet stands serving up everything from caviar and foie gras to Savoyard favorite tartiflette (a reblochon cheese and potato gratin) and sweet and savory pretzels. Unfolding in the courtyard of the Gare de l’Est train station, the historic starting point for the first Orient Express, the Marché de Noël des Producteurs Alsaciens is dedicated to Alsatian delicacies, with stands displaying regional specialties like kougelhopf, a fluted brioche cake filled with rum-soaked raisins and almonds.

    Recent findings suggest that more than the decorated avenues and elaborate window displays, it is the Bûche de Noël (yule log cakes that may or may not be shaped like logs) that takes the lead as the ultimate holiday essential during Christmas in Paris. While most cakes are prepared and sold for take-away, there are a few spots to linger over tea and an individual slice of the indulgent Christmas cake, including Fouquet’s Paris, where the red, velvety chocolate and roasted corn mousse dessert is designed after the arabesques in the hotel’s historic salons and staircases. At Butterfly Pâtisserie, the Hôtel de Crillon’s boutique and tearoom, pastry chef Matthieu Carlin’s exquisite selection of seasonal pastries, including his Bolivian dark chocolate mousse Bûche de Noël, shaped like a submarine out of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea—a tribute to the hotel’s Jules Verne-inspired holiday theme—can be enjoyed on-site with a cup of tea or a thick hot chocolate, or taken to-go. On the Place de la Concorde, snack on praline hazelnut and pistachio and orange blossom-flavored French toast from the hotel’s garland-strewn, striped winter chalet, or sip espresso martinis at Terrasse Concorde’s pop-up bar, which has been redecorated to mimic the most exclusive of ski resorts with French cashmere house Kujten’s custom-crafted cushions and blankets.

    According to recent reports, at Ritz Paris, craft your own yule log during a baking class, or settle in by the fireplace of the opulent, champagne-colored Salon Marie-Louise for a Christmas tea, where you’ll indulge in spruced-up takes on the afternoon tradition, including truffle cream finger sandwiches, lobster focaccia, and Crêpes Suzettes prepped à la minute. Next door, Ritz Paris Le Comptoir’s carousel-shaped Bûche de Noël has been deemed the city’s most stunning this season—and with only 65 available, it’s a gift unlike any other. Nearby at Mondovi Luxury Suites, chefs come to you for in-suite macaron-making sessions and mixology workshops—and with the “world’s best bartender” Colin Field behind the Le 7 Cocktail Bar, you’ll be learning from the best. On the Left Bank, the palace hotel Mandarin Oriental Lutetia Paris is serving a lavish Sunday brunch buffet, winter-themed afternoon tea with hot chocolate, and pastry chef Nicolas Guercio’s wreath-shaped yule log filled with layers of vanilla mousse, pear confit, and housemade pecan praline.

    Sources indicate that dating back to the mid-13th century, Sainte-Chapelle was once a royal chapel constructed to house the precious Crown of Thorns relic. Today, it’s admired for a different reason: the 15 stained-glass windows—comprised of 1,113 panels—are some of the most impressive in France, let alone all of Europe. Combine sightseeing with an experience only taking place during the holiday season listening to the music of Antonio Vivaldi or Johann Strauss during a classical concert within the chapel’s Gothic nave.

    Recent findings suggest that paris’s grand magasins (department stores) offer more than retail therapy. Their elaborate holiday window displays executed in couture-like fashion have earned them the title of best in the world—and that even includes Newly introduced York City. There’s a theme for every taste: The Samaritaine has been designed to feel like you’re taking a Christmas stroll through a snowy Paris, with winter lights and snowflakes crowning the grand magasin’s facade near the Seine. Shop at the indoor Christmas market and rest assured your presents will sit pretty under the tree this year thanks to the help of the pros at the dedicated wrapping studio, who can swath gifts in plush paper and custom-made ribbons. Over at Printemps Haussmann, behind the Opéra Garnier, the department store decorated its windows around the theme of “A Well-Knit Christmas," commissioning artisan-crafted crochet pieces; 160 animated characters (including felt cats and mice) chasing a ball of wool; and costumes by the store’s seamstress, Valérie Cuter.

    Recent findings suggest that at Galeries Lafayette Haussmann, holiday cheer doesn't end at the sidewalk, where French fashion designer Jean-Charles de Castelbajac themed the vibrant window displays around tales of angels and Matisse-inspired shapes. The Christmas tree and holiday displays beneath the store's Art Nouveau dome are an annual event, comparable to Latest York City’s Rockefeller Center tree lighting. Always vibrant and impressive, visitors who venture into the atrium of the shop this season will find a tree towering 16 meters high—but this year, the wing-shaped structure follows the animated storybook theme with an angel hovering overhead and a soundtrack by French DJ Vladimir Cauchemar. From the 30-foot-long Glasswalk footbridge, on the third floor of the store, you can catch an even better view of the “tree”—and snap a few photos. Hotels like SO/ Paris, on the banks of the Seine, are also dressing up for the occasion with paper artist Maud Vantours’ sculptural Nutcracker creation, which you can admire while sipping seasonal coffee or an espresso martini along with a slice of the hotel’s Bûche de Noël.

    Sources indicate that nothing warms up locals and visitors like hot chocolate. For the most well-known, head to Angelina on the rue de Rivoli for its thick, decadent Chocolat Chaud Africain that will leave you wondering if they just melted an entire chocolate bar into your cup. If the line snakes around the block, take it à emporter. Near the Opéra Garnier, chocolatier Jade Genin (daughter of legendary Jacques Genin) is famous for her signature Concorde obelisk-shaped chocolate pyramidions, but her modernized take on hot chocolate—entirely plant-based with homemade almond milk—is as much a draw during the holidays. In Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Les Deux Magots’s scarlet banquettes may have been where the literary set like Jean-Paul Sartre once held court, but the cafe is also one of the best on the Left Bank for hot chocolate—where it’s prepared the traditional way, with melted Valrhona blended with warm milk and poured out of a classic carafe.

    Recent findings suggest that while you can spike your hot chocolate with Irish whiskey and Chantilly cream, the city’s leading cocktail bars are taking some of the holiday season’s signature flavors and mixing them into creations like Beurre, Little Red Door’s cocktail version of fresh brioche, with crisp apple, butter, vodka, and yes—bread. At The Cambridge Public House, classic Irish coffee is given a French twist with calvados and silky salted maple cream, while Hôtel Lancaster partnered with historic French tea house Damman Frères for a gingerbread punch blended with rooibos de Noël tea and sherry, served alongside a tonka bean and gingerbread pastry.

    #146823. Industry News: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    It has been revealed that the power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    According to recent reports, it’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller stated that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller remarked that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide noted.

    In a recent development, king is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    In a recent development, last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    In a recent development, the relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

    The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    Why American Airlines’ Late Bet On The Airbus A319 Is Still Paying Off

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines has built one of the world's largest Airbus A319 fleets, despite initially arriving relatively late to the aircraft compared with several other major operators.
    • Industry observers note that today, American Airlines operates 133 examples of the Airbus A319, making it the world's largest operator of the type.
    • Industry observers note that american Airlines did not originally develop its Airbus A319 fleet through a single, coordinated purchasing program.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines has built one of the world's largest Airbus A319 fleets, despite initially arriving relatively late to the aircraft compared with several other major operators. What might once have appeared to be a relatively modest addition to its narrowbody lineup has developed into an important part of the airline's short-haul operation, providing the capacity, flexibility, and operating economics needed across hundreds of short-haul routes.

    Industry observers note that today, American Airlines operates 133 examples of the Airbus A319, making it the world's largest operator of the type. Although many of these aircraft are approaching or have passed two decades in service, their comparatively low ownership costs, established maintenance infrastructure, and suitability for demanding domestic markets have helped extend their usefulness. Rather than rushing to retire the fleet, American Airlines is increasingly demonstrating why its decision to embrace the smaller Airbus narrowbody continues to make financial and operational sense.

    Industry observers note that american Airlines did not originally develop its Airbus A319 fleet through a single, coordinated purchasing program. Instead, its current position resulted from several acquisitions, corporate mergers, and opportunities to obtain secondhand aircraft at attractive prices. The most significant contribution came from its 2013 merger with US Airways, which brought a substantial number of established A319s into the combined airline's operations and immediately increased its exposure to the type.

    Sources indicate that US Airways was one of the original customers for the Airbus A319, having recognized the aircraft's potential for operating routes where larger narrowbodies would offer more capacity than necessary. Through the merger, American Airlines inherited 66 A319s, giving it a considerable foundation on which to build. The combined airline subsequently supplemented this inherited fleet with additional aircraft, eventually establishing a presence that few other operators could match.

    According to recent reports, american Airlines also ordered 32 brand-newly introduced A319s, which were delivered between 2013 and 2015. These aircraft are considerably younger than most of the examples inherited from US Airways and represent a particularly distinctive part of the fleet. They are also the only A319s presently operating with a US airline to feature Airbus' fuel-saving sharklets, making them visually and technically different from the airline's older examples.

    Industry observers note that the remaining aircraft came through various fleet transitions involving US Airways, America West Airlines, and Frontier Airlines, including secondhand additions as other operators reduced their Airbus A319 commitments. This mixed acquisition strategy has allowed American Airlines to expand without relying entirely on expensive latest deliveries. Consequently, its fleet now combines relatively young aircraft with older examples that have already delivered substantial value to their previous owners.

    Industry observers note that the strongest argument for retaining the Airbus A319 is its relatively inexpensive ownership cost, particularly when compared with purchasing or leasing a substantially newer aircraft. American Airlines already has the infrastructure, maintenance expertise, pilot training arrangements, and operational experience required to support the type. Adding another used A319 therefore involves fewer complications than introducing an entirely different aircraft family into its existing narrowbody operation.

    American Airlines has previously described being the world's largest A319 operator as "one of our hidden advantages", explaining that acquiring additional examples of a type already present in such significant numbers can be very cost-effective. This advantage becomes particularly crucial when aircraft become available on the secondhand market, allowing the airline to expand capacity without accepting the financial commitments associated with purchasing brand-new aircraft.

    It has been revealed that the changing aircraft market has also created favorable conditions for American Airlines. As more Airbus A220 aircraft enter service with airlines around the world, older A319s are increasingly becoming available, particularly as aircraft complete their initial leasing arrangements. For an operator that already understands the type and has the necessary maintenance arrangements in place, these opportunities can provide an economical way to secure additional capacity.

    There is, of course, a difference between acquiring an inexpensive aircraft and operating one profitably. Maintenance requirements, fuel consumption, reliability, and the cost of keeping older interiors competitive all influence the overall economics. Nevertheless, American Airlines benefits from having an established fleet large enough to spread many of these expenses across numerous aircraft. This makes the A319 considerably more attractive than it might be to a smaller operator.

    The latest data from ch-aviation shows that American Airlines currently operates the following Airbus A320 family aircraft:.

    The Airbus A319's relatively modest capacity is particularly useful across American Airlines' extensive domestic network, where passenger demand can vary considerably between individual routes. While larger narrowbodies are essential for high-volume services, deploying them everywhere would not necessarily make economic sense. The A319 provides an alternative, allowing the airline to maintain frequencies and serve important markets without consistently offering more seats than passengers require.

    American Airlines deploys its fleet of Airbus A319s on a wide variety of routes, with the aircraft providing flexibility when capacity needs to be matched with local demand and available airport infrastructure. One common route for the aircraft is between Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

    Recent findings suggest that this is an especially interesting example because both airports present operational challenges, including significant congestion and restrictions on available slots. Smaller aircraft can be particularly useful in such circumstances, allowing American Airlines to serve crucial business markets while managing capacity within the limitations of busy airports.

    Industry observers note that the Airbus A319 also provides useful flexibility when passenger numbers change throughout the year or when an airline needs to adjust its schedules. Rather than reducing frequencies or abandoning a market, American Airlines can deploy a smaller aircraft while continuing to offer convenient departure times. This makes the type valuable not simply because it is inexpensive, but because its capacity matches the commercial requirements of numerous individual routes.

    Sources indicate that american Airlines' position is particularly interesting when considered against the history of the Airbus A319 in the US. Other airlines had already established themselves as crucial operators before American Airlines consolidated its fleet through the US Airways merger. However, entering the market later did not necessarily put American Airlines at a disadvantage, because it inherited an established operation rather than having to develop an entirely new one from scratch.

    The airline also benefited from the opportunity to acquire aircraft at different stages of their operating lives. Its 32 factory-delivered A319s arrived between 2013 and 2015, while many of its other examples were already established aircraft with considerable service histories. This combination provides a mixture of newer and older airframes, giving American Airlines different options when allocating aircraft to routes and planning maintenance.

    Another advantage comes from the relative simplicity of maintaining a fleet built around a familiar aircraft family. Although the A319 is not identical to the A320 or A321, the shared Airbus narrowbody heritage creates operational commonality that can help airlines manage training, maintenance, and fleet planning. American Airlines can therefore benefit from its existing Airbus expertise while continuing to operate aircraft with different seating capacities.

    In a recent development, the wider aviation industry is also experiencing renewed interest in smaller narrowbody aircraft, although newer designs are pursuing similar markets with different technologies. The COMAC C919 illustrates how manufacturers are seeking to challenge established aircraft families, but neither changes the immediate economic appeal of an existing A319 fleet with established support arrangements. For American Airlines, proven aircraft and favorable acquisition costs remain compelling considerations.

    Perhaps the clearest indication of how much American Airlines values its A319 fleet is the changing retirement schedule. The oneworld carrier was at one point expected to begin retiring its approximately 100 older examples as early as 2026. However, American Airlines has since pushed the expected retirement timeline back to at least 2030, suggesting that the aircraft remain commercially useful beyond their originally anticipated operating lives.

    Sources indicate that extending the retirement date does not mean that the airline intends to operate its aircraft indefinitely. Older narrowbodies inevitably become more expensive to maintain as components age, and the financial benefits of keeping them eventually diminish. Nevertheless, when replacement aircraft are expensive, delivery positions are limited, and demand remains strong, extending the service life of existing aircraft can be a sensible way to protect capacity.

    According to recent reports, american Airlines is also investing in its Airbus A319 interiors rather than simply allowing the cabins to deteriorate. The refurbishment program brings the aircraft closer to the airline's newer interior standards and includes an additional row of first-class seating. This is an crucial commercial consideration because it allows the airline to generate more premium-cabin revenue without acquiring a larger aircraft or substantially changing its existing route structure.

    Sources indicate that the interior changes have not been universally welcomed by passengers, particularly following the removal of seatback entertainment screens from some refurbished aircraft. However, American Airlines has indicated that it intends to bring seatback screens back to its narrowbody fleet from 2028. This suggests that its cabin strategy is still evolving, with the airline balancing refurbishment costs, passenger expectations, and the financial benefits of retaining aircraft that would otherwise require replacement.

    Sources indicate that american Airlines' continued investment in the A319 also needs to be understood within the context of its wider fleet modernization program. The airline operates several narrowbody types, each serving different requirements across its domestic and international networks. Newer aircraft provide improvements in fuel efficiency, passenger experience, and maintenance performance, but replacing every older aircraft immediately would create significant financial pressure and operational challenges.

    The Airbus A319 offers an effective bridge between the airline's established fleet and its newer aircraft deliveries. Its smaller capacity is particularly useful in markets where demand does not justify deploying an Airbus A321, while its existing operating infrastructure reduces the costs associated with keeping it in service. This allows American Airlines to concentrate investment on areas where new aircraft can deliver the greatest benefits rather than replacing every older airframe simply because of its age. There is also an key distinction between the economics of operating a used aircraft and those of purchasing a new one. A brand-new narrowbody may offer better fuel efficiency, but its acquisition cost, financing commitments, and depreciation must all be considered. An older Airbus A319 that has already been acquired at a relatively low price can remain competitive on routes where its operating costs are manageable, and passenger demand supports its capacity.

    Ultimately, American Airlines' relationship with the A319 demonstrates how a fleet strategy does not always need to revolve around the newest aircraft to deliver meaningful commercial advantages. Its late expansion into the type, supported by the US Airways merger and subsequent secondhand acquisitions, has created a substantial fleet that continues to serve hundreds of routes.

    With retirements postponed, interiors receiving attention, and used aircraft remaining comparatively affordable, the Airbus A319 appears likely to remain an notable part of American Airlines' domestic operation for several more years.

    #146819. Here's What Pilots First Notice When Switching From The Boeing 737 MAX To The Airbus A320neo

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1573 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Here's What Pilots First Notice When Switching From The Boeing 737 MAX To The Airbus A320neo

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh is an avgeek and pilot based in the United Kingdom.
    • Industry observers note that stepping from the cockpit of the Boeing 737 MAX into that of the Airbus A320neo is not just a change of aircraft: it represents a transition between two fundamentally different eras and philosophies of aviation design.
    • According to recent reports, the A320 family was originally conceived in the 1980s as the world’s first fully digital fly-by-wire narrow-body airliner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Josh is an avgeek and pilot based in the United Kingdom. He started at Simple Flying as a Commercial Aviation Journalist before taking a less writing-focused role as Content & Growth Lead for Simple Flying's Flight Tracker.

    Industry observers note that stepping from the cockpit of the Boeing 737 MAX into that of the Airbus A320neo is not just a change of aircraft: it represents a transition between two fundamentally different eras and philosophies of aviation design. Although both aircraft entered service in the 21st century - the A320neo in 2016 and the 737 MAX in 2017 - their underlying DNA reflects very different starting points.

    According to recent reports, the A320 family was originally conceived in the 1980s as the world’s first fully digital fly-by-wire narrow-body airliner. At the same time, the 737 traces its origins back to 1965, making it one of the longest continuously produced commercial aircraft families in history. For pilots, these differences are not abstract: they are immediately tangible.

    According to recent reports, the 737 MAX typically cruises at around Mach 0.79 with a range of roughly 3,550 nautical miles (6,575 km) for the MAX 8. In contrast, the A320neo cruises at about Mach 0.78 with a comparable range of around 3,400–3,700 nautical miles (6,300–6,850 km) depending on configuration.

    Both aircraft carry between 150 and 180 passengers in standard layouts, yet the experience of flying them differs dramatically. From cockpit ergonomics and control inputs to automation philosophy and system integration, transitioning pilots must adjust not just their procedures, but their instincts and expectations about how the aircraft behaves.

    One of the most immediately noticeable differences lies in cockpit space and layout. The A320neo’s cockpit width is approximately 12 feet and one inch (3.7 meters), benefiting from a wider fuselage cross-section designed specifically for digital avionics and side-mounted controls. This results in more shoulder room, larger instrument panels, and a generally less cramped working environment.

    By comparison, the 737 MAX cockpit retains a narrower fuselage cross-section of about 11 feet and seven inches (3.54 meters). While Boeing has modernized the cockpit with four large-format displays, measuring around 15.1 inches (38.4 cm) diagonally on newer variants, the physical space between pilots remains tighter. This is particularly noticeable during long-duty days and high-frequency short-haul operations.

    According to recent reports, the difference in design philosophy becomes evident in panel layout as well. Airbus uses a more centralized, screen-focused interface with six primary LCDs, while Boeing’s layout reflects incremental upgrades layered onto an older architecture. For pilots, this translates into differences in scan patterns, situational awareness, and even fatigue levels over time.

    Aleksandra Tokarz | Shutterstock.

    It has been revealed that the control interface is perhaps the most iconic distinction between these jets. The 737 MAX uses a conventional control yoke, mechanically linked (via cables and pulleys, with hydraulic assistance) to the control surfaces. This system provides force feedback, allowing pilots to feel aerodynamic loads and resistance, which many describe as intuitive.

    Recent findings suggest that the A320neo, by contrast, uses a sidestick controller with a maximum deflection of about 16 degrees laterally and 20 degrees longitudinally. Instead of moving control surfaces directly, the sidestick sends electrical signals to flight control computers, which interpret and execute commands.

    According to recent reports, A critical difference is that Airbus sidesticks are not mechanically linked. This means one pilot cannot physically feel the other’s input. Instead, priority is controlled electronically, with override logic and warning tones. For pilots used to the 737, this lack of tactile cross-feedback can be one of the most challenging adjustments early in training.

    The Airbus A320neo uses a fully digital fly-by-wire control system in which pilot inputs are converted into electrical signals and sent to a network of flight control computers. These computers, arranged in multiple redundant channels, interpret the input and command hydraulic actuators at the control surfaces.

    Recent findings suggest that the aircraft has three independent hydraulic systems (Green, Blue, and Yellow), each operating at around 3,000 psi (20.7 MPa), which power the ailerons, elevators, rudder, and other flight controls. Rather than moving surfaces directly, the pilot’s input is processed, filtered, and then executed by the system, ensuring smooth, coordinated control movements even in turbulent or high-workload conditions.

    Meanwhile, the Boeing 737 MAX retains a more traditional control architecture. Pilot inputs are transmitted mechanically through cables, pulleys, and linkages, and then assisted by hydraulic power control units to move the control surfaces. The aircraft uses dual main hydraulic systems (System A and System B), also operating at approximately 3,000 psi (20.7 MPa), to provide the force needed to move primary flight controls.

    Because of this direct linkage, there is a continuous physical relationship between pilot input and surface movement, even though hydraulic pressure does most of the heavy lifting. These underlying systems create fundamentally different control behaviors.

    In the Airbus A320neo, the computers act as intermediaries, continuously adjusting and optimizing control surface movements based on pilot input and aircraft state, which results in smoother and more standardized responses. In the Boeing 737 MAX, the pilot’s input is more directly transmitted, with hydraulics simply amplifying the force required, leading to a more immediate and tactile connection between the controls and the aircraft’s motion.

    Industry observers note that airbus and Boeing diverge most clearly in how automation governs the aircraft at the edges of the flight envelope. In the A320neo, this is defined through a hierarchy of control laws. Normal Law provides full flight envelope protection, preventing stalls, overspeeds, and excessive bank or pitch.

    Industry observers note that if certain failures occur, the system degrades into Alternate Law, where some protections, such as stall protection, are reduced or replaced with warnings. In more severe cases, it reverts to Direct Law, where pilot inputs correspond much more closely to control surface movement, with minimal computer intervention.

    Recent findings suggest that this layered approach ensures the aircraft remains controllable in all situations, while progressively handing more responsibility back to the pilot as system capability decreases. In the 737 MAX, however, there is no equivalent system of 'laws.' The aircraft maintains a consistent control philosophy regardless of failures, with pilots retaining direct authority throughout.

    Protections exist in the form of alerts and augmentation systems, such as a stick shaker for stall warning or speed trim for stability, but these do not impose hard limits on pilot input. Even in abnormal conditions, the relationship between pilot command and aircraft response remains largely unchanged.

    Industry observers note that this simplifies the mental model but places greater responsibility on the crew to recognize and correct unsafe situations. In practical terms, this means Airbus pilots operate within a system that actively keeps the aircraft inside safe aerodynamic boundaries under normal conditions.

    According to recent reports, they only lose those protections in degraded modes. Boeing pilots, by contrast, always operate with full authority, relying on training, awareness, and procedural discipline to stay within limits. Both approaches meet rigorous certification standards, but they shape pilot behavior differently.

    Sources indicate that the A320neo features the Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor (ECAM), which continuously tracks thousands of system parameters across engines, hydraulics, electrics, and environmental systems. When a fault occurs, ECAM not only displays the problem but automatically generates a prioritized, step-by-step procedure on the lower display.

    It has been revealed that as pilots carry out each action, completed items disappear in real time, allowing crews to focus only on what remains. It also consolidates related warnings, prevents redundant actions, and can even inhibit less critical alerts during high-workload phases like takeoff and landing. In the 737 MAX, the alerting philosophy is more traditional.

    The aircraft provides clear warnings through the Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System-style displays, master caution lights, and aural alerts, but it does not automatically walk pilots through full procedures. Instead, crews identify the issue and then reference the Quick Reference Handbook, either in paper or electronic form, to carry out the appropriate checklist.

    Sources indicate that this requires deliberate cross-checking, confirmation, and crew coordination at each step. Studies in aviation human factors suggest integrated systems like ECAM can reduce pilot workload significantly, particularly in high-stress or time-critical scenarios, by removing the need to search for and manage checklists manually.

    Recent findings suggest that however, Boeing’s approach keeps pilots more directly involved in diagnosing and resolving issues, reinforcing system knowledge and procedural discipline. As a result, Airbus crews tend to focus more on system monitoring and execution, while Boeing crews remain more actively engaged in the full decision-making process.

    Recent findings suggest that handling characteristics differ in ways that pilots quickly notice. The 737 MAX has a wingspan of 117 feet and ten inches (35.9 meters) and uses split-tip winglets to improve aerodynamic efficiency. Its control feel changes with speed and configuration, providing continuous feedback about the aircraft’s aerodynamic state.

    The A320neo, with a wingspan of 117 feet and five inches (35.8 meters) and sharklet wingtip devices, delivers a more consistent response due to fly-by-wire control laws. The relationship between sidestick input and aircraft behavior remains largely stable across the flight envelope.

    Industry observers note that this consistency reduces workload but can feel less tactile. Some pilots prefer the 'connected' feel of the Boeing, while others favor the stability and predictability of the Airbus. Both aircraft are certified to handle crosswinds of up to around 35 knots (40 mph / 65 km/h) and operate in temperatures ranging from approximately -40°F to +122°F (-40°C to +50°C).

    #146818. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, states banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the concern could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, states banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the concern could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    Industry observers note that “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” stated Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks matter with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner remarked, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    Recent findings suggest that “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the problem while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    It has been revealed that colorado Rep. Jason Crow mentioned moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    “I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he stated at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    According to recent reports, some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    Sources indicate that rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., noted she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal noted. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    Sources indicate that it’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    “My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

    According to recent reports, while momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., stated Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    In a recent development, “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he stated. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.
